questions.stem: All monitors are functioning during a stable MAC case, but the anesthesia provider leaves the room briefly. Which requirement of ASA Standard I is no longer met?
options: Continuous waveform capnography with audible alarms
Pulse oximetry with a variable-pitch tone
The ECG with ST-segment analysis enabled
questions.explanation: Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout every anesthetic. No device replaces the provider.

questions.stem: A 3-hour open laparotomy has continuous ECG, SpO2, ETCO2, and BP every 5 minutes, but no temperature data. Which ASA Standard II domain is missing?
questions.explanation: Standard II requires continual evaluation of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature; a long open abdomen with fluid shifts clearly calls for temperature monitoring.

questions.stem: During stable GA without an arterial catheter, the NIBP cuff is changed from cycling every 5 minutes to every 10 minutes because repeated readings are normal. Which statement is correct?
options: This violates the requirement to determine and evaluate arterial pressure and heart rate at least every 5 minutes
The longer interval is acceptable once three consecutive pressures are stable
Ten-minute cycling is acceptable if continuous ECG and pulse oximetry are present
The interval is acceptable unless vasoactive drugs are being administered
questions.explanation: BP and HR must be determined and evaluated at least every 5 minutes. The notes add it may be more frequent, never less.

questions.stem: Beyond ECG and blood pressure, which FOUR methods satisfy ASA 2.3 for evaluating circulation? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The standard lists pulse palpation, heart sound auscultation, arterial tracing, ultrasound peripheral pulse, or pulse plethysmography/oximetry.

questions.stem: During prone positioning after induction, ECG electrodes are removed and not replaced for 10 minutes while pulse oximetry and NIBP continue. Which requirement is specifically unmet?
options: Continuous ECG display from the beginning of anesthesia until preparing to leave the anesthetizing location
ECG monitoring only from incision until closure
ECG monitoring only during induction and emergence
ECG monitoring only in patients with known cardiovascular disease
questions.explanation: ASA 2.3 requires continuous ECG display from the beginning of anesthesia until preparing to leave the room.

questions.stem: During every general anesthetic using an anesthesia machine, which oxygen-safety monitor is specifically required?
options: An O2 analyzer in the breathing system with a low-O2 alarm
Arterial blood gases at least once per hour of anesthesia
A pulse oximeter with an alarm set to 90% or lower
A paramagnetic analyzer placed in the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: Inspired oxygen concentration in the breathing system must be measured by an analyzer with a low-concentration alarm.

questions.stem: During GA, inspired O2 is 50% and expired O2 is 45% with stable ventilation. What best explains the difference?
options: Expected oxygen uptake by the patient
A circuit leak drawing in room air
Hypoxic gas delivery from the machine
questions.explanation: Expired O2 is lower than inspired O2 because the patient consumes oxygen. Monitoring both shows what goes in and what comes out.

questions.stem: During GA with an ETT, capnography alarms repeatedly and the provider considers relying only on chest rise and breath sounds. What does ASA 2.2 require?
options: Continual expired CO2 monitoring plus clinical signs
Expired CO2 at intubation and extubation
Expired CO2 when SpO2 falls below 92%
questions.explanation: Clinical signs help, but ASA 2.2 requires continual expired CO2 monitoring.

questions.stem: The first case after a weekend shows a persistently elevated inspired CO2 baseline. The machine had been left with high fresh-gas flow. What is the most likely cause?
options: Desiccated or exhausted absorbent allowing rebreathing
Hypoxic gas delivery from the pipeline
Dilution of the sample by room air
Complete loss of the capnography sampling line
questions.explanation: Desiccated or exhausted CO2 absorbent allows rebreathing, seen as a nonzero inspired CO2 baseline.

questions.stem: Which patients most clearly require temperature monitoring under ASA 2.4: a 15-minute knee scope, a 4-hour open colectomy, and a cardiac case with planned cooling?
options: The colectomy and the cardiac case
The colectomy only, since cooling is monitored by the perfusionist
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring is required when significant changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected, as with long open cases and planned cooling.

questions.stem: Rocuronium was given, but no twitch monitor is used and extubation is based only on a 5-second head lift. Which AANA monitoring expectation is not met?
options: NM monitoring when reversal will not be given
NM monitoring for cases over 2 hours
questions.explanation: AANA 8e requires monitoring NM response for depth and recovery, using quantitative monitoring when available.

questions.stem: Before reversing rocuronium, which method gives the most reliable evidence of neuromuscular recovery?
options: A visual twitch count at the ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: Quantitative monitoring with a TOF ratio is preferred because qualitative methods miss residual block.

questions.stem: A patient under deep sedation becomes progressively hypercapnic while SpO2 remains normal on supplemental oxygen. Which monitoring failure most closely mirrors the recurring problem identified in hypoventilation closed claims?
options: Failure to obtain intermittent arterial blood gases
Failure to use invasive blood pressure monitoring
questions.explanation: Every hypoventilation claim involved failure to monitor ventilation.

questions.stem: A closed-claims dataset reports that more than 65% of claims involved errors in judgment. In a review of 200 similar claims, approximately how many would be expected to fall into that category?
questions.explanation: More than 65% of closed claims involved errors in judgment.

questions.stem: Which category of event is the most common preventable source of anesthesia claims and payouts?
questions.explanation: Respiratory events are the most common preventable cause of claims and payouts.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, bilateral chest movement appears present and SpO2 remains 100% from preoxygenation, but no sustained exhaled CO2 waveform appears. Which safety advance is designed to prevent the catastrophic error most associated with this pattern?
options: Routine capnographic confirmation to detect esophageal intubation
Processed EEG monitoring to detect awareness
questions.explanation: Capnography significantly reduced unrecognized esophageal intubation.

questions.stem: An overnight provider has been awake 20 hours, loud music is playing, and phone use occurs between vital checks. Which THREE factors impair vigilance? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: External distractions, human factors such as fatigue, and self-initiated distractions such as phones all impair vigilance.

questions.stem: After a hypoxic event, the team initially attributes the problem to a ventilator defect, but testing shows normal equipment function and review reveals an incomplete pre-use check. Which closed-claims lesson BEST applies?
options: User error and failure to check equipment are more common contributors than true device malfunction
Device malfunction remains the most likely cause of anesthesia adverse events
A normal post-event device test excludes any equipment-related contribution
Equipment checks add little because most failures are unpredictable
questions.explanation: Adverse outcomes are rarely due to device malfunction; user error and failure to check are far more common.

questions.stem: A preventable event follows incorrect use of the anesthesia workstation rather than failure of the device itself. Which equipment category has been disproportionately represented in closed claims from misuse?
questions.explanation: Misuse of gas delivery systems was 3x more prevalent among closed claims.

questions.stem: A provider unfamiliar with the ventilator skips the machine check because it was used yesterday. Which two human factors most commonly underlie equipment mishaps?
questions.explanation: Most equipment-related mishaps come from unfamiliarity and failure to check, not device failure.

questions.stem: The first anesthetic of the day begins without a workstation checkout because the machine functioned normally overnight. Which AANA requirement is most directly violated?
options: Verification of anesthesia equipment function before each anesthetic
Use of patient-specific audible alarm limits
questions.explanation: AANA Standard 5 requires verifying anesthesia equipment function before each anesthetic.

questions.stem: SpO2 alarm volume is muted and the low limit is set to 70%. Which AANA standard is violated?
questions.explanation: Standard 9 requires appropriate alarm limits and audible warnings.

questions.stem: During surgery, the pulse-oximeter tone progressively drops in pitch while the provider is looking at the surgical field. What information is being conveyed before the numerical SpO2 is viewed?
options: A falling oxygen saturation through the variable-pitch pulse tone
A change in blood pressure through pulse-tone frequency
A capnography alarm encoded in the pulse tone
An ECG rhythm change independent of oxygen saturation
questions.explanation: Variable-pitch tones let you hear desaturation without looking at the monitor.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions most strongly promote alarm fatigue? (Select 2)
options: Difficulty localizing alarms in a noisy room
Turning alarm volumes to a clearly audible level
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue comes from frequent noncritical or false alarms and difficulty localizing alarms in noise. Audible, well-set alarms reduce it.

questions.stem: Which THREE consequences are typical of alarm fatigue? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue leads to ignoring or disabling alarms and missed critical events.

questions.stem: A healthy athlete has a baseline HR of 48 and repeatedly triggers a low-HR alarm set at 50. What is the best response?
options: Adjust the limit while keeping it within practice standards
Turn the HR alarm off since the rate is baseline
Keep the default limit and adjust the volume
Turn the low HR alarm to 40 for every athlete
questions.explanation: Alarm limits can be individualized, but the new settings must still meet practice standards.

questions.stem: SpO2 suddenly reads 86% with a noisy pleth waveform. Because prior alarms were artifact, the provider silences it without examining the patient or sensor. Which cognitive failure is MOST important?
options: Prematurely attributing a potentially valid alarm to artifact without verification
Correct application of patient-specific alarm limits
Failure to use an arterial catheter
questions.explanation: Assuming artifact without checking the patient is cognitive bias. Every alarm must be evaluated.

questions.stem: A low-ETCO2 alarm sounds briefly during a previously stable anesthetic and then the value returns to baseline without intervention. What is the safest response?
options: Determine why the alarm occurred despite spontaneous normalization
Assume transient artifact because the value recovered
Change the alarm threshold before evaluating the patient
Increase fresh-gas flow and wait for recurrence
questions.explanation: Every alarm needs evaluation of its cause, even when it self-resolves.

questions.stem: A trainee says, 'The monitors will tell me if anything is wrong.' What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Monitors must be interpreted and acted on by the provider
Technology alone prevents most patient harm
Monitors reduce the need for clinical assessment
Alarms replace a systematic sweep of the room
questions.explanation: Monitors are tools. Their data must be interpreted and acted upon by the provider.

questions.stem: A stable anesthetic becomes unexpectedly hypotensive shortly after surgical positioning. The provider deliberately scans the patient, monitors, airway, machine, IVs, and surgical field in a fixed sequence. What is the principal advantage of this technique?
options: It reduces omission by forcing a systematic search across patient, equipment, and field
It replaces the need to respond to individual alarms
It establishes the cause before any intervention is started
It satisfies the formal surgical time-out requirement
questions.explanation: A sweep is a methodical scan of patient, equipment, and field.

questions.stem: Which THREE senses are explicitly part of proactive vigilance beyond monitor data? (Select 3)
options: Monitor trends reviewed after the case
questions.explanation: Use sight, hearing, smell, touch, and technology.

questions.stem: During a machine sweep several hours into a case, which FOUR items should be checked? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: The machine sweep includes vaporizer level, water trap, absorbent color, and the capnogram.

questions.stem: Which TWO patient-positioning checks belong in a routine anesthesia sweep? (Select 2)
options: Eyes taped and free from pressure
questions.explanation: The patient sweep covers positioning, eyes, pressure points, secure lines, and functional IVs.

questions.stem: Which FOUR surgical-field elements belong in the anesthesia sweep? (Select 4)
options: Blood loss in laps, suction, and floor
questions.explanation: The field sweep covers case status, blood loss, drapes, surgeon communication, and fire risk.

questions.stem: During room preparation, suction and airway equipment are ready, but the workstation has not yet been checked. Using MS MAID, which setup element remains the first priority?
questions.explanation: MS MAID: Machine, Suction, Monitors, Airway, IV, Drugs. The machine check comes first.

questions.stem: Under MS MAID, what should be included in the 'Machine' check beyond the workstation itself?
options: Full check plus a bag-mask and spare O2 cylinder
The vaporizer level and ventilator settings
The CO2 absorbent and water trap
questions.explanation: The machine portion includes a full checkout plus a resuscitation bag-mask and a spare O2 cylinder.

questions.stem: Immediately after induction, the patient regurgitates. A Yankauer is present but produces no suction because the canister valve was never opened. Which preinduction verification would have prevented this failure?
options: Confirm suction is assembled, on, functional, and immediately reachable
Confirm only that a Yankauer is physically present
Test suction only in patients undergoing RSI
Verify that the suction canister is empty
questions.explanation: Suction must have canister, tubing, and Yankauer, and be on, working, and in reach.

questions.stem: Which FOUR airway items should be immediately available in the room under MS MAID? (Select 4)
options: Extra blade, handle, and ETT sizes
questions.explanation: The room should have an LMA, extra blades/handles, ETT sizes, stylet, lubricant, syringe, OPA, and NPA.

questions.stem: Even for a routine elective ETT case, which rescue airway should already be available in the room?
options: A cricothyrotomy kit opened on the field
questions.explanation: An LMA should always be available as a rescue device when mask ventilation or intubation fails.

questions.stem: During a power failure, battery-powered airway equipment is unusable. Which MS MAID preparation step was missed?
questions.explanation: The MS MAID setup includes making sure spare batteries and battery-powered equipment work.

questions.stem: A patient enters the OR for induction and no standard monitors are yet attached. According to the lecture sequence, which monitor should be applied first?
questions.explanation: The sequence starts with SpO2, then preoxygenation by mask, then BP, then ECG with a baseline strip.

questions.stem: A healthy patient has SpO2 100% after 30 seconds of preoxygenation, but expired oxygen is only 72%. Which finding BEST indicates that adequate denitrogenation has not yet occurred?
options: Expired oxygen remains below the target of about 90%
Heart rate is unchanged from baseline
questions.explanation: Preoxygenate 3–5 minutes or until expired O2 ≥90%.

questions.stem: A patient cannot hold the mask during preoxygenation and both of your hands are needed elsewhere. What can maintain a reliable seal?
options: A loose mask with higher flow
An oral airway without a mask
questions.explanation: Head straps maintain the mask seal while your hands are free for other tasks.

questions.stem: After LMA placement, chest excursion and bilateral breath sounds appear normal and SpO2 remains 100%. What additional finding is required to confirm ventilation through the device?
options: Sustained identification of exhaled CO2 in addition to clinical assessment
questions.explanation: ASA requires verification by clinical assessment and identification of expired CO2.

questions.stem: For an ETT or SGA, how long should continuous ETCO2 monitoring remain in use?
options: From placement until removal or transfer to postop care
From placement until the end of surgery
During the first 30 minutes after placement
questions.explanation: ETCO2 is monitored from placement until extubation/removal or initiating transfer.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, the capnogram suddenly disappears because the breathing circuit separates from the ventilator. Which required safety feature should independently alert the provider to this event?
options: A second capnograph on the expiratory limb
questions.explanation: ASA requires a disconnect detection device with an audible alarm during mechanical ventilation.

questions.stem: During deep propofol sedation, a patient receives supplemental oxygen and maintains SpO2 99% while respiratory effort progressively decreases. Which monitoring combination is required to detect the problem before oxygen desaturation?
options: Qualitative assessment of ventilation plus continuous exhaled CO2 monitoring
questions.explanation: Moderate/deep sedation requires qualitative signs and continuous exhaled CO2.

questions.stem: During regional anesthesia with minimal or no sedation, what level of ventilation monitoring is required?
options: Continual observation of qualitative clinical signs
Arterial blood gases drawn at the start and every hour
questions.explanation: With minimal or no sedation, qualitative clinical signs are required.

questions.stem: Which TWO bedside findings can support airway placement while capnography provides definitive confirmation? (Select 2)
options: A normal blood pressure after intubation
Smell of volatile at the patient's nose
questions.explanation: Condensation and chest excursion verify airway placement along with breath sounds and ETCO2. Blood pressure says nothing about tube position.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, the first two capnograms appear appropriate. According to this monitoring lecture, what additional evidence is required before tube placement is considered confirmed?
options: A third full consecutive ETCO2 waveform
One waveform with ETCO2 above 20 mm Hg
questions.explanation: This lecture requires three full consecutive ETCO2 waveforms. (Phases of GA used six; know which your instructor tests.)

questions.stem: During a stable anesthetic, the provider notices a new sweet volatile odor near the workstation before any gas-monitor alarm changes. Which principle of vigilance does this illustrate?
options: Sensory information such as smell can reveal a volatile-agent leak before monitor trends change
Odor confirms that the vaporizer concentration is accurate
Smell can confirm correct endotracheal-tube position
Volatile odor is expected whenever low-flow anesthesia is used
questions.explanation: Smell can detect volatile leaks from the vaporizer or circuit.

questions.stem: Two hours into an uneventful anesthetic, every displayed value has remained stable. Which change in monitoring behavior is appropriate?
options: None; vigilance remains continuous despite prolonged stability
Reduce active surveillance and rely on alarms
Perform systematic sweeps only during induction and emergence
Delegate physiologic surveillance to the automated record
questions.explanation: Vigilance must remain constant throughout the anesthetic.

questions.stem: A facility protocol permits NIBP cycling every 10 minutes during uncomplicated GA. What should the anesthesia provider do?
options: Follow the applicable professional minimum requiring arterial pressure and heart rate evaluation at least every 5 minutes
Follow the facility protocol because local policy supersedes professional standards
Use 10-minute intervals whenever continuous ECG is present
Use 10-minute intervals until the patient becomes unstable
questions.explanation: ASA and AANA standards define the standard of care, which requires BP at least every 5 minutes.

questions.stem: A regional anesthetic is planned for a case that could become longer or more invasive than expected. What does the lecture's principle of 'GETA backup to everything' require?
options: Prepare the equipment and plan needed for prompt conversion to general anesthesia
Induce general anesthesia before performing every regional technique
Avoid regional anesthesia whenever conversion is possible
Keep airway equipment outside the room until conversion is requested
questions.explanation: Every plan needs GETA as backup.

questions.stem: Which THREE broad drug categories are included in MS MAID preparation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Drugs span preop, blocks, induction, maintenance, emergence, emergency, transport, and PACU.

questions.stem: For a trauma laparotomy, which THREE elements belong in IV setup planning? (Select 3)
options: A fluid warmer and adequate IV size and number
An arterial line for every case
questions.explanation: IV setup includes fluid type, lines, pumps, rapid infuser, warmer, and appropriate access.

questions.stem: Which combination best matches the standard monitor list presented on the MS MAID slide?
options: ECG, NIBP, ETCO2, SpO2, EMG, Fi and Fe gases
ECG, arterial line, SpO2, and processed EEG
questions.explanation: Standard ASA monitors listed are ECG, NIBP, ETCO2, SpO2, electromyography, and inspired/expired gases.

questions.stem: During a seemingly stable anesthetic, the surgeon announces that major vascular clamping will occur in 2 minutes. Why is continuous awareness of surgical progress a monitoring skill rather than merely a workflow concern?
options: It allows anticipation of changes in stimulation, blood loss, hemodynamics, and anesthetic requirements
It allows anesthesia to control the surgeon's operative pace
It primarily determines the next case start time
It replaces the need to monitor current physiologic trends
questions.explanation: Knowing case status helps anticipate critical points.

questions.stem: A new OR installs advanced automated monitors and assumes adverse events will decline without changing clinician workflow. Which limitation of monitoring technology is MOST important?
options: Data and alarms improve safety only when clinicians recognize, interpret, and act on them
Correct alarm settings eliminate the need for active surveillance
Automated monitoring removes most need for clinical assessment
Documentation quality is the principal determinant of whether monitors prevent harm
questions.explanation: Technology supports care, but harm is prevented only when providers interpret and act on the data.

questions.stem: PIP rises from 20 to 35 cmH2O while plateau pressure remains 17 cmH2O and tidal volume is unchanged. Which mechanical change BEST explains the new pressure gradient?
options: Increased resistive pressure from greater airway resistance
Increased elastic recoil from lower lung compliance
questions.explanation: PIP reflects dynamic compliance, which includes airway resistance; a stable plateau shows static compliance is unchanged.

questions.stem: Tidal volume is 500 mL, plateau pressure 25 cmH2O, and PEEP 5 cmH2O. What is static compliance?
questions.explanation: Static compliance = Vt ÷ (Pplat − PEEP) = 500 ÷ 20 = 25 mL/cmH2O.

questions.stem: A mechanically ventilated patient has PIP 21 cmH2O and plateau pressure 19 cmH2O. What does the small pressure difference suggest?
options: Little additional resistive pressure, consistent with relatively normal airway resistance
questions.explanation: Normally PIP is equal to or only slightly above plateau pressure.

questions.stem: PIP and plateau pressure both increase by 10 cmH2O after steep Trendelenburg while tidal volume and inspiratory flow remain unchanged. Which mechanism is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: A parallel rise in PIP and plateau means higher Vt or lower pulmonary compliance.

questions.stem: PIP increases from 22 to 40 cmH2O while plateau remains 18 cmH2O after the patient's head is repositioned. Which problem should be investigated FIRST?
options: Increased airway resistance such as ETT kinking or obstruction
questions.explanation: PIP up without plateau change means increased airway resistance or inspiratory gas flow.

questions.stem: A pressure trace shows PIP 38 and plateau 19 cmH2O. Which problem does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: Increased airway resistance, such as a kink or bronchospasm
Decreased lung compliance from abdominal insufflation
A larger tidal volume set on the ventilator
A circuit leak reducing the delivered volume
questions.explanation: The big gap between PIP and plateau points to resistance, not compliance. Kinks, secretions, and bronchospasm fit.

questions.stem: A pressure trace shows PIP 36 and plateau 33 cmH2O. Which problem does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: Decreased compliance, such as insufflation or pneumothorax
Increased resistance from a kinked ETT
Secretions partially occluding the tube lumen during inspiration
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together, so compliance fell or Vt rose. Pneumoperitoneum, pneumothorax, or position change fit.

questions.stem: PIP rises abruptly from 22 to 38 cmH2O while plateau remains unchanged. Breath sounds are diminished but present bilaterally. Which bedside maneuver most directly distinguishes intraluminal ETT obstruction from other resistance causes?
options: Pass a suction catheter through the ETT
Increase inspiratory flow and observe PIP
Obtain a chest radiograph before manipulating the airway
questions.explanation: A suction catheter quickly identifies kinks or secretions.

questions.stem: Which TWO problems raise PIP without significantly changing plateau pressure? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Resistance problems such as a kinked tube or bronchospasm raise PIP alone. Larger tidal volumes and compliance changes raise both PIP and plateau.

questions.stem: Which FOUR conditions can raise both PIP and plateau pressure? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Compliance changes and larger volumes raise both pressures.

questions.stem: A trainee interprets a pressure-volume loop as though pressure were on the vertical axis. Which correction is required before using loop slope to judge compliance?
options: Pressure is horizontal and volume is vertical
Pressure is vertical and volume is horizontal
Flow is horizontal and pressure is vertical
Flow is vertical and volume is horizontal
questions.explanation: The P-V loop plots volume on the vertical axis against airway pressure on the horizontal axis.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg, a pressure-volume loop shifts so that greater pressure is required to deliver the same volume. Which mechanical property has worsened?
questions.explanation: P-V loops primarily assess compliance; flattening toward the pressure axis means lower compliance.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient develops prolonged expiration and a scooped expiratory limb on the flow-volume loop while plateau pressure remains unchanged. Which mechanical abnormality is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Flow-volume loops primarily assess resistance; a scooped expiratory limb suggests obstruction.

questions.stem: Which FOUR conditions decrease respiratory compliance on a pressure-volume loop? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Decreased compliance means more pressure for the same volume: PE, bronchoconstriction, PTX, insufflation, inadequate relaxation.

questions.stem: A patient with severe emphysema requires relatively little pressure to generate a given tidal volume compared with baseline. Which change in elastic mechanics does this represent?
options: Increased airway resistance with unchanged compliance
questions.explanation: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue, increasing compliance so more volume enters for the same pressure.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, the same 500-mL tidal volume requires substantially more pressure. How should the pressure-volume loop change?
options: It flattens toward the pressure axis
It rotates toward the volume axis
It opens into a wide hysteresis
questions.explanation: Lower compliance means more pressure for the same volume, flattening the loop toward the pressure axis.

questions.stem: After the patient's head is turned, the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop flattens and PIP rises while plateau remains stable. Which mechanism BEST unifies these findings?
options: Increased airway resistance from partial ETT obstruction
questions.explanation: Higher resistance reduces expiratory flow, flattening the expiratory limb of the flow-volume loop.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions primarily increase airway resistance rather than reduce compliance? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Kinks and bronchospasm raise resistance on the flow-volume loop. Raised abdominal pressure, fibrosis, and obesity reduce compliance instead.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has prolonged expiration, air trapping, high residual lung volume, and a scooped expiratory flow-volume limb. Which pattern BEST fits these findings?
options: Obstructive physiology with impaired expiratory flow
Restrictive physiology with impaired inspiratory expansion
questions.explanation: Obstructive disease limits expiratory flow and traps air, increasing lung volumes.

questions.stem: A patient has markedly reduced lung volumes but the basic contour of the flow-volume loop is preserved rather than scooped. Which pattern is MOST consistent?
questions.explanation: Restrictive disease limits lung expansion, producing smaller volumes with preserved flow shape.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions produce a restrictive flow-volume pattern? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Fibrosis and obesity are restrictive. COPD, asthma, bronchospasm, and kinks increase resistance.

questions.stem: During ventilation, the expiratory flow-volume limb begins flattening before the high-pressure alarm activates. What is the clinical advantage of recognizing this loop change?
options: It can identify evolving resistance abnormalities before threshold alarms are reached
It directly measures arterial oxygen tension
It eliminates the need for airway-pressure monitoring
It distinguishes every cause of hypoxemia without further assessment
questions.explanation: Spirometry loops show changes in compliance and resistance in real time, often before alarms trigger.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, higher airway pressure is required to generate smaller tidal volumes and the pressure-volume loop shifts toward the pressure axis. Which pattern does this most closely mimic?
options: Obstructive mechanics from isolated airway resistance
questions.explanation: Insufflation pushes up the diaphragm and mimics restriction.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the Y-piece. Which THREE alarms should be expected first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms are low PIP, low exhaled Vt, and low ETCO2.

questions.stem: Which THREE alarm trends together should immediately suggest a circuit disconnection? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms are low PIP, low exhaled Vt, and low ETCO2.

questions.stem: During volume-controlled ventilation, PIP, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 all drift slightly downward together but remain above alarm thresholds. Which developing problem should be considered?
questions.explanation: Small leaks cause subtle decreases in PIP, exhaled volume, or ETCO2 before alarms trigger.

questions.stem: Beyond disconnect detection, which FOUR ventilator alarms help identify dangerous circuit or patient conditions? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Other ventilator alarms include high PIP, high PEEP, sustained high pressure, negative pressure, and low O2 supply pressure.

questions.stem: During a routine ventilator sweep, which TWO parameter groups should be reviewed? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Ventilator parameters include mode, tidal volume and frequency, minute ventilation, peak and mean pressures, PEEP, and loops.

questions.stem: Which THREE gases are routinely displayed as both inspired and expired concentrations? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: The monitor shows Fi and Et for O2, CO2, air, volatile agent, and N2O.

questions.stem: After steep Trendelenburg, plateau pressure rises from 18 to 26 cmH2O with unchanged tidal volume and inspiratory flow. Which mechanical change is MOST likely?
questions.explanation: Positioning changes respiratory compliance; a parallel rise in plateau and peak pressure points to compliance.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, PIP rises from 22 to 32 and plateau from 18 to 28. Which cause best fits this parallel increase?
options: A circuit leak at the Y-piece lowering delivered volume
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together, consistent with reduced compliance from insufflation.

questions.stem: PIP rises from 22 to 40 while plateau remains 18; suctioning retrieves thick secretions. Which mechanism caused the pressure change?
questions.explanation: PIP up with stable plateau suggests resistance; secretions fit.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, a previously paralyzed patient begins coughing against the ventilator and both peak and plateau pressures rise. Which cause BEST explains the transient fall in compliance?
options: Inadequate neuromuscular relaxation increasing chest-wall stiffness
questions.explanation: Inadequate relaxation increases chest wall stiffness and decreases compliance.

questions.stem: In ARDS, plateau pressure approaches 30 cmH2O while tidal volume is being adjusted. Why are continuous pressure-volume and flow-volume displays useful in addition to numeric alarms?
options: They reveal evolving overdistension, derecruitment, and mechanical changes before or between alarm thresholds
questions.explanation: Real-time loops help detect overdistension or derecruitment and guide settings to prevent lung injury.

questions.stem: An oxygen analyzer has rapid response, no consumable electrochemical cell, and detects oxygen because of its attraction to a magnetic field. Which technology is being used?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers exploit oxygen's attraction to a magnetic field.

questions.stem: During maintenance, an oxygen analyzer becomes progressively sluggish after prolonged service because its sensing element is consumed by the measurement reaction. Which sensor type fits this failure mode?
questions.explanation: Galvanic cells generate current from an oxygen-dependent reaction and are consumed.

questions.stem: A polarographic Clark electrode is used for oxygen analysis. Which reaction occurs at the cathode?
questions.explanation: Polarographic (Clark) sensors reduce oxygen at the cathode: O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.

questions.stem: During checkout, the oxygen sensor is found in the expiratory limb. Why should it instead sample the inspired limb?
options: To detect a hypoxic gas mixture before or as it is delivered to the patient
To measure the patient's oxygen consumption directly
questions.explanation: The O2 sensor belongs in the inspired limb to detect hypoxic gas delivery to the patient.

questions.stem: A removable galvanic oxygen sensor reads 18% while exposed to room air during checkout. What should occur before relying on it clinically?
options: Calibrate it against room air at approximately 21% oxygen
questions.explanation: Galvanic sensors are calibrated to room air (21%) daily and after prolonged use.

questions.stem: Which response-time and accuracy specifications best match an acceptable oxygen analyzer?
options: Response in about 2–10 seconds with ±2% accuracy
questions.explanation: Oxygen analyzers target about 2–10 second response time and ±2% accuracy.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the oxygen pipeline remains normal but inspired O2 concentration gradually decreases. Which mechanism makes continuous inspired-O2 analysis essential?
options: Patient oxygen consumption can exceed replacement sufficiently to lower circuit FiO2
Low fresh-gas flow directly creates oxygen toxicity
Low flow causes oxygen analyzers to read falsely high
Nitrogen washout accelerates as fresh-gas flow falls
questions.explanation: With low fresh gas flow, oxygen consumption can reduce the circuit FiO2.

questions.stem: FiO2 remains 0.50, but SpO2 falls to 84% after right mainstem intubation. What limitation of inspired-O2 monitoring does this illustrate?
options: Adequate FiO2 does not guarantee arterial oxygenation
Inspired O2 monitoring detects intubation errors
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 monitoring confirms delivery, not uptake; patient factors such as endobronchial intubation can still cause hypoxemia.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects at the Y-piece. ETCO2 and exhaled tidal volume fall, but the inspired-O2 reading initially remains normal. Why?
options: Fresh gas can continue passing the inspired O2 sensor despite loss of connection to the patient
A functioning O2 analyzer cannot detect any circuit problem
The O2 sensor automatically substitutes room-air values during disconnection
Inspired-O2 alarms are disabled whenever capnography is active
questions.explanation: The inspired limb still contains fresh gas after a disconnect, so the O2 reading may stay normal.

questions.stem: A galvanic oxygen sensor has a much shorter service life than expected despite correct calibration. Which repeated exposure can accelerate depletion of the cell?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide exposure shortens galvanic sensor life.

questions.stem: During airway laser surgery, SpO2 is adequate on FiO2 0.60. Before laser activation, which change most directly reduces oxidizer contribution to airway-fire risk?
options: Reduce FiO2 to the lowest concentration that safely maintains oxygenation
Increase FiO2 to shorten laser activation time
Increase fresh-gas flow while maintaining FiO2 0.60
Replace oxygen with a higher concentration of nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Oxygen enrichment in the airway during laser or cautery use raises fire risk.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has SpO2 99% despite suspected carbon monoxide exposure; another patient after topical benzocaine remains near SpO2 85% despite high FiO2. Which explanation BEST fits both findings?
options: Conventional pulse oximetry may read COHb as oxyhemoglobin, whereas MetHb drives the ratio toward about 85%
Both findings are best explained by anemia
Carbon monoxide drives SpO2 toward 85%, whereas MetHb falsely raises it toward 100%
Both dyshemoglobins are accurately distinguished by standard two-wavelength pulse oximetry
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish COHb (falsely high) and MetHb (drives readings toward 85%). Co-oximetry is needed.

questions.stem: A patient with severe ARDS has FiO2 0.80 confirmed by the circuit analyzer but PaO2 remains very low. What does this discrepancy demonstrate?
options: Inspired-O2 monitoring confirms delivery, not effective arterial oxygenation
The FiO2 analyzer must be malfunctioning whenever PaO2 is low
Inspired-O2 monitoring should be replaced by intermittent ABGs
FiO2 and PaO2 should remain numerically proportional in ARDS
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 confirms delivery; pair it with SpO2 or ABGs to confirm oxygenation.

questions.stem: Which statement about clinical contraindications to inspired-O2 monitoring is correct?
options: It is contraindicated with nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 monitoring has no clinical contraindications.

questions.stem: An oxygen analyzer detects pressure changes caused by oxygen interacting with a switched magnetic field. Which analyzer is this?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic analyzers detect pressure changes in switched magnetic fields.

questions.stem: Which oxygen sensor measures current generated as O2 diffuses across a membrane and is reduced at an electrode?
questions.explanation: Polarographic sensors measure current as O2 diffuses through a membrane.

questions.stem: During machine checkout, the inspired-O2 analyzer displays the expected concentration but its low-concentration alarm is disabled. Which safety check remains incomplete?
options: Verification of both analyzer calibration and the low-O2 alarm function/limit
Verification of only the high-O2 alarm
Verification of the pipeline gauge only
questions.explanation: Verify low-O2 alarm limits and calibration during daily checkout.

questions.stem: A gas analyzer identifies CO2, N2O, and volatile agents by wavelength-specific light absorption. Which technology is being used?
questions.explanation: Modern gas analyzers mainly use infrared absorption, measuring how strongly each gas absorbs specific wavelengths.

questions.stem: At approximately which infrared wavelength does CO2 absorb strongly for capnographic measurement?
questions.explanation: CO2 absorbs infrared light strongly at about 4.3 microns. The 660 and 940 nm wavelengths are used by pulse oximeters.

questions.stem: During stable GA, PaCO2 is 41 mmHg and ETCO2 is 36 mmHg. In a healthy supine patient, how should this gradient be interpreted?
options: Typical, because PaCO2 commonly exceeds ETCO2 by about 2–10 mmHg
Abnormally wide, indicating major dead-space ventilation
Reversed, because ETCO2 should normally exceed PaCO2
questions.explanation: The gradient is typically around 5 mmHg, from anatomic dead space.

questions.stem: Why will a standard infrared gas analyzer fail to measure xenon?
options: Xenon does not absorb infrared light
Xenon absorbs at the same wavelength as CO2
Xenon is too soluble to sample
questions.explanation: Infrared analysis requires gases that absorb infrared light; noble gases such as xenon do not.

questions.stem: At the beginning of expiration, the capnogram remains at baseline before the rapid upstroke begins. What gas source dominates this initial exhaled volume?
options: Alveolar gas with the highest CO2 concentration
Fresh inspired gas entering the lungs
questions.explanation: Phase A–B is the exhalation of dead space gas that contains no CO2.

questions.stem: At what point on a normal time capnogram is ETCO2 measured?
options: At the end of the alveolar plateau immediately before inspiration
At the start of the expiratory upstroke
At the midpoint of the alveolar plateau
At the end of the inspiratory downstroke
questions.explanation: Point D is the highest CO2 value at end-expiration: the ETCO2.

questions.stem: What physiologic event produces the rapid inspiratory downstroke on a normal capnogram?
options: Fresh gas is inspired and measured CO2 rapidly falls toward baseline
Alveolar gas is sampled at a stable plateau
Dead-space gas is exhaled before CO2 appears
Mixed dead-space and alveolar gas causes the expiratory upstroke
questions.explanation: D–E is the inspiratory downstroke as fresh gas is entrained.

questions.stem: Two patients have similar ETCO2 values, but one has a near-vertical expiratory upstroke while the other has a prolonged sloped upstroke. Which physiologic difference most directly explains the morphology?
options: The uniformity and rate of alveolar emptying
questions.explanation: The B–C slope reflects the evenness of alveolar emptying; uneven emptying from obstruction slopes the upstroke.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has an alveolar plateau that continues to slope upward late in expiration instead of flattening. What produces this pattern?
options: Late emptying of poorly ventilated units with heterogeneous V/Q relationships
questions.explanation: An upward-sloping plateau reflects V/Q mismatch, with slow-emptying units releasing higher CO2 late in expiration.

questions.stem: After intubation of an asthmatic patient, PIP increases, plateau pressure remains near baseline, and the capnogram develops a shark-fin contour. Which process BEST unifies these findings?
questions.explanation: A slow upstroke with a shark-fin shape indicates obstruction such as COPD or bronchospasm.

questions.stem: Serial capnograms in a patient with bronchospasm show progressively greater rounding between the expiratory upstroke and alveolar plateau. What does this trend suggest?
options: Worsening airflow obstruction and increasingly heterogeneous emptying
Increasing anatomic dead space without obstruction
questions.explanation: The more rounded the upstroke and plateau corner, the greater the obstruction.

questions.stem: A normally shaped capnogram shows progressively rising ETCO2. Which TWO mechanisms best explain this? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: A normal shape with rising values means hypoventilation or increased CO2 production.

questions.stem: Which TWO events can transiently raise ETCO2 by washing accumulated CO2 back into circulation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Tourniquet release and aortic unclamping wash CO2 from ischemic tissue, transiently raising ETCO2. Hyperventilation lowers it.

questions.stem: A previously normal capnogram abruptly becomes flat immediately after the table is rotated. Which response is BEST?
options: Rapidly assess the patient/airway, breathing circuit, pulmonary perfusion, and sampling system rather than assuming a single cause
Increase minute ventilation before checking the airway
Wait for SpO2 to fall to distinguish artifact from disconnection
questions.explanation: Sudden waveform loss can mean disconnection, obstruction, arrest, or sampling failure, all of which need immediate evaluation.

questions.stem: After intubation, three sustained capnograms are present and bilateral breath sounds are heard. Which conclusion is justified by the CO2 finding alone?
options: Tracheal rather than persistent esophageal ventilation is supported, but tube depth still requires assessment
questions.explanation: Stable ETCO2 supports non-esophageal placement but does not rule out endobronchial or shallow placement.

questions.stem: During stable GA, FiO2, ETCO2, and end-tidal sevoflurane all fall abruptly at the same moment without a corresponding clinical change. Which explanation should be investigated first?
options: A shared gas-sampling or analyzer problem
questions.explanation: When every measured gas changes together, suspect the sampling line or equipment. A single gas changing suggests the patient.

questions.stem: During stable GA, ETCO2 abruptly decreases from 36 to 20 mmHg while FiO2 and end-tidal sevoflurane remain unchanged and the capnogram persists. Which category is more likely than a shared analyzer failure?
options: A physiologic reduction in CO2 delivery to the lungs, such as reduced pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: A change in one gas points to patient physiology, such as reduced pulmonary perfusion.

questions.stem: Which FIVE conditions increase dead space and widen the PaCO2–ETCO2 gradient? (Select 5)
options: An adult circuit in a small child
questions.explanation: Dead space and V/Q mismatch increase the gradient: PE, emphysema, OLV, low CO.

questions.stem: A small child is connected to equipment that adds excessive apparatus dead space. PaCO2 rises while sampled ETCO2 underestimates the arterial value. Which mechanism contributes to the discrepancy?
options: Greater dead-space fraction and dilution of alveolar exhaled gas
Faster sidestream sampling caused by smaller airways
questions.explanation: Using adult circuits in pediatrics increases dead space and dilutes the sample.

questions.stem: A premature infant has extremely low minute ventilation. Why can a conventional sidestream capnograph itself become clinically significant?
options: Its sampling flow may remove a substantial fraction of the infant's minute ventilation and distort the sample
Sidestream systems sample too little gas to detect neonatal CO2
The sampling line adds only inspiratory resistance without removing gas
questions.explanation: Sidestream sampling of up to about 200 mL/min can be a significant fraction of an infant's ventilation and distort readings.

questions.stem: A 900-g infant receives 40 mL tidal volumes at 6 breaths/min while a sidestream analyzer removes 150 mL/min. Approximately what fraction of the calculated 240 mL/min minute ventilation is being sampled?
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation is 6 × 40 = 240 mL/min; 150 mL/min is about 60% of it, which distorts readings and ventilation.

questions.stem: Condensation repeatedly occludes a sidestream sampling line. Which simple positioning change reduces water entry?
options: Keep the sampling port pointing up
Lower the sampling line below the circuit
questions.explanation: Positioning the sampling line above the circuit reduces water entering the line.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the capnogram inspiratory baseline rises to 6 mmHg and no longer returns to zero. Which abnormality is demonstrated regardless of its cause?
questions.explanation: A baseline that does not return to zero means the patient is inhaling CO2 (rebreathing).

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 is elevated. Which THREE circuit causes should be checked first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: An elevated inspiratory baseline means rebreathing from exhausted absorbent, faulty valves, low FGF, or miscalibration.

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 remains above zero on low fresh-gas flow. Which cause best fits this rebreathing pattern?
options: Exhausted CO2 absorbent or a sticking valve
A partially kinked ETT with a shark-fin upstroke
questions.explanation: The baseline does not return to zero, indicating rebreathing.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, inspired CO2 rises to 7 mmHg; the absorber is exhausted and fresh-gas flow is 0.5 L/min. Which immediate response BEST addresses the likely sources of rebreathing?
options: Increase fresh-gas flow while checking/replacing absorbent and assessing unidirectional valves
Increase tidal volume without changing the circuit
questions.explanation: Rebreathing from exhausted absorbent and low fresh gas flow is fixed by raising flow and checking absorbent and valves.

questions.stem: Which FOUR problems can cause ETCO2 to fall abruptly to near zero with loss of waveform? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Sudden loss suggests malposition, severe hypotension, massive PE, cardiac arrest, or disconnection.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, a notch appears in the alveolar plateau at the same time the patient begins making inspiratory efforts. What does this waveform change indicate?
options: A curare cleft from returning spontaneous respiratory effort
questions.explanation: A curare cleft shows spontaneous effort against the ventilator, often from wearing-off NMB.

questions.stem: A plateau notch appears long after the last rocuronium dose. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Returning spontaneous effort as blockade wears off
Bronchospasm from surgical stimulation at a light plane
questions.explanation: A notch in the plateau is a curare cleft, showing spontaneous effort.

questions.stem: A persistent curare cleft appears as neuromuscular blockade wears off, but surgery still requires immobility. Which response is MOST appropriate after confirming anesthetic depth and the need for paralysis?
options: Redose neuromuscular blocker and continue quantitative monitoring
questions.explanation: A curare cleft shows the patient is breathing against the ventilator, which may need more paralytic or deeper anesthesia.

questions.stem: Small regular oscillations appear near end-expiration and are synchronized with the ECG. What are they?
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic oscillations come from heart and great vessel contractions moving gas at end expiration.

questions.stem: During volume-controlled ventilation, the capnogram becomes triangular, exhaled tidal volume falls, and a hissing sound is heard near the airway. Which problem BEST explains all three findings?
questions.explanation: A sloping, triangular trace with low exhaled volume suggests a leak in the circuit or cuff.

questions.stem: At a high respiratory rate in a patient with stiff lungs, expiration does not fully complete before the next breath and the capnogram develops a pigtail appearance. Which mechanism BEST fits?
options: Breath stacking related to poor compliance and inadequate expiratory time
Normal ventilation at high respiratory rate
questions.explanation: A pigtail capnogram suggests poor compliance or breath stacking.

questions.stem: Which FIVE problems can produce a completely flat capnogram? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: A flat trace indicates esophageal intubation, disconnection, apnea, or arrest.

questions.stem: A patient receives propofol TIVA with an ETT and controlled ventilation. Which gas-monitoring statement is correct?
options: End-tidal volatile-agent concentration is not relevant to propofol delivery, but continuous ETCO2 monitoring remains required
Capnography is unnecessary because no volatile anesthetic is administered
Expired volatile-agent monitoring determines propofol effect-site concentration
Pulse oximetry can replace capnography during TIVA
questions.explanation: No gas in means no gas out, but ETCO2 is still required.

questions.stem: During low-flow sevoflurane anesthesia, the vaporizer is set to 2% but measured end-tidal sevoflurane changes slowly after adjustments. Why is expired-agent monitoring particularly useful?
options: Circuit and alveolar agent concentrations can lag or differ from the vaporizer setting, so measured expired concentration guides titration
It replaces inspired-O2 monitoring at low flows
questions.explanation: Expired agent monitoring helps titrate volatile agents, especially with low flows.

questions.stem: In which TWO situations is capnography routinely required by the lecture standards? (Select 2)
options: Recovery on a postoperative surgical floor
questions.explanation: Capnography is standard during GA and required during moderate and deep sedation.

questions.stem: During a stable anesthetic, ETCO2 suddenly falls from 36 to 20 mmHg while a recognizable waveform remains and ventilation settings are unchanged. Which physiologic problem should be high on the differential?
options: An abrupt reduction in pulmonary blood flow, such as pulmonary embolism
questions.explanation: A sudden fall with waveform present suggests reduced perfusion.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 28 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 50 mmHg. Which interpretation is MOST appropriate?
options: The markedly widened gradient suggests increased dead space or V/Q mismatch
The gradient is normal for a healthy anesthetized adult
The finding primarily indicates CO2 rebreathing
The sampling line must be completely disconnected
questions.explanation: A 22 mmHg gradient indicates increased dead space or V/Q mismatch.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation, ETCO2 is 31 mmHg while PaCO2 is 46 mmHg despite stable minute ventilation. Why can ETCO2 substantially underestimate PaCO2 in this setting?
options: Increased V/Q mismatch and dead-space fraction widen the arterial-to-end-tidal CO2 gradient
One-lung ventilation sharply reduces systemic CO2 production
One-lung ventilation necessarily causes sampling-line dilution
questions.explanation: OLV increases dead space and V/Q mismatch, lowering ETCO2 relative to PaCO2.

questions.stem: A neonate with a cuffless ETT has adequate chest excursion and a PaCO2 of 42 mmHg, but sidestream ETCO2 is unexpectedly low. Which explanation BEST fits the discrepancy?
options: Leak around the cuffless tube plus dilution/removal from a relatively high sampling flow
Increased neonatal CO2 production should make ETCO2 falsely low
A normal neonatal PaCO2–ETCO2 gradient is routinely this large
CO2 rebreathing from exhausted absorbent lowers ETCO2
questions.explanation: Neonatal cuffless tubes and high sidestream rates can produce falsely low ETCO2.

questions.stem: After CO2 pneumoperitoneum, PIP and plateau pressure rise together while ETCO2 gradually increases despite unchanged minute ventilation. Which combination BEST explains the changes?
options: Reduced respiratory compliance plus systemic absorption of insufflated CO2
Increased airway resistance plus reduced CO2 production
Improved compliance plus decreased pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: Insufflation reduces compliance and CO2 is absorbed from the abdomen, raising ETCO2.

questions.stem: During hip arthroplasty, ETCO2 abruptly falls from 38 to 24 mmHg while the waveform remains recognizable and BP falls to 75/40 mmHg. Ventilator settings are unchanged. Which mechanism BEST explains the ETCO2 change?
options: Reduced CO2 delivery to the lungs from decreased pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: A lower ETCO2 with a preserved waveform reflects reduced perfusion, as in hypotension or embolism.

questions.stem: During a previously stable anesthetic, the capnogram abruptly disappears immediately after patient repositioning. SpO2 is still 99%. What should be done FIRST?
options: Assess the patient, airway, and ventilation connection immediately rather than waiting for desaturation
Replace the water trap before examining the patient
questions.explanation: Loss of ETCO2 is an emergency until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: During an otherwise stable anesthetic, ETCO2 rises from 38 to 60 mmHg with a normal waveform despite unchanged minute ventilation; temperature and heart rate are also rising. Which cause is MOST concerning?
options: Markedly increased CO2 production such as malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with normal shape suggests increased CO2 production or hypoventilation.

questions.stem: In a healthy anesthetized patient with good V/Q matching, ETCO2 is 35 mmHg. Which physiologic value does this most closely approximate?
questions.explanation: ETCO2 approximates alveolar CO2 in patients with normal V/Q matching.

questions.stem: Why should a normal capnogram return to a zero baseline during inspiration?
options: The patient inhales fresh gas without CO2
CO2 is absorbed by the lungs during inspiration
The sampling line closes during inspiration
The monitor resets with each breath
questions.explanation: During inspiration, fresh gas containing no CO2 fills the sampling site, returning the baseline to zero.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly falls to near zero, but arterial pressure and ECG remain stable and the patient continues to receive mechanical breaths. Which cause should move higher on the differential?
options: Capnography sampling failure or a circuit/airway disconnection affecting the sample
Massive pulmonary embolism causing cardiovascular collapse
questions.explanation: Loss of ETCO2 with stable BP often points to disconnection or sampling issues.

questions.stem: A patient develops wheezing, rising PIP with unchanged plateau pressure, and a progressively sloped expiratory capnogram. Which waveform description BEST matches the process?
options: Shark-fin morphology from expiratory airflow obstruction
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm causes a shark-fin shape.

questions.stem: During a long humidified case, the capnogram becomes intermittently damped and then disappears while ventilation and hemodynamics remain unchanged. Which technical problem is MOST likely?
options: Condensation obstructing the sidestream sampling line
Capnography becoming unreliable solely because case duration is long
Humidification causing systematic low arterial CO2
questions.explanation: Sampling lines can occlude with condensation, causing erratic or lost readings.

questions.stem: What alarm characteristic is required for ETCO2 monitoring?
options: It must be audible to the anesthesia team
It may be paused during repositioning
It must be visible but may be silenced
It must be visible on the screen
questions.explanation: The ETCO2 alarm must be audible to the anesthesia provider or team.

questions.stem: Before the patient is connected, the capnograph displays a persistent 4-mmHg baseline despite fresh gas flowing through the circuit. Which explanation is MOST likely?
options: Exhausted absorbent caused by the patient
questions.explanation: An elevated baseline with no patient connected points to a calibration error.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, PIP rises while plateau pressure remains stable and the capnogram becomes shark-fin shaped. Which problem category BEST unifies these findings?
options: Increased airway resistance from bronchospasm or partial ETT obstruction
questions.explanation: Shark-fin shape with high pressures suggests obstruction.

questions.stem: Immediately after prone positioning for spine surgery, PIP rises to 38 cmH2O, plateau remains near baseline, and a new shark-fin capnogram appears. Which cause should be investigated FIRST?
options: Partial ETT kinking or obstruction related to positioning
questions.explanation: A kinked ETT causes an obstructive shark-fin pattern with high PIP.

questions.stem: Immediately after tourniquet release, ETCO2 transiently rises despite unchanged ventilation. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Washout of accumulated CO2 from the previously ischemic limb into the circulation
Acute increase in alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: Tourniquet release returns CO2 from ischemic tissue.

questions.stem: Immediately after attempted intubation, several small CO2 waveforms appear but rapidly diminish to zero with continued ventilation. Which interpretation is MOST concerning?
options: Transient washout of swallowed/gastric CO2 after esophageal intubation
questions.explanation: Gastric CO2 can produce a few small waveforms that rapidly disappear with esophageal placement.

questions.stem: A low-ETCO2 alarm activates during a previously stable anesthetic. Which initial approach BEST avoids anchoring on a single cause?
options: Assess the patient and airway while rapidly checking circuit/sampling integrity and perfusion
Increase respiratory rate before assessing the cause
Check only the sampling line because low ETCO2 is usually technical
questions.explanation: Every capnography alarm requires prompt evaluation of patient, airway, circuit, and perfusion.

questions.stem: During propofol-opioid sedation, respiratory rate falls from 14 to 6/min and ETCO2 rises progressively while SpO2 remains 98% on supplemental oxygen. Which process is occurring?
options: CO2 rebreathing from an exhausted absorber
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with slower RR suggests hypoventilation.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has prolonged expiration, a sloped alveolar plateau, and elevated ETCO2. Which mechanism BEST explains the waveform morphology?
options: Heterogeneous emptying from airflow obstruction and V/Q mismatch
questions.explanation: COPD causes V/Q mismatch and a sloped plateau.

questions.stem: During acute pulmonary embolism, PaCO2 remains 42 mmHg while ETCO2 falls from 36 to 24 mmHg. Which change in respiratory physiology BEST explains the widened gradient?
options: Increased alveolar dead space from ventilated but underperfused lung
questions.explanation: PE increases dead space, lowering ETCO2 and widening the gradient.

questions.stem: For ischemia detection during vascular surgery, which ECG lead is most sensitive according to the lecture data?
questions.explanation: In the Landesberg study, V3 detected ischemia earliest and most often (86.8%), followed by V4 and V5.

questions.stem: In the cited vascular-surgery study, what proportion of ischemic events appeared as ST depression?
questions.explanation: 97% of ischemic events showed ST depression, not elevation.

questions.stem: A patient with coronary disease requires both reliable atrial/rhythm surveillance and sensitive perioperative ischemia monitoring. Which lead strategy BEST addresses both goals according to the lecture?
options: Monitor lead II for rhythm together with a precordial ischemia-sensitive lead such as V3
Use lead II alone because rhythm and ischemia sensitivity are equivalent
Use V1 alone for both atrial activity and ischemia
questions.explanation: Lead II is best for rhythm; V3 is most sensitive for ischemia.

questions.stem: An irregular rhythm with abnormal P waves develops intraoperatively. Which lead best evaluates atrial activity?
questions.explanation: Lead II aligns with atrial depolarization, so it is best for rhythm and atrial arrhythmia analysis.

questions.stem: A patient's preoperative ECG shows reproducible ST depression in V4 and V5 during prior ischemic episodes. Which intraoperative strategy best applies ECG 'fingerprinting'?
options: Prioritize monitoring leads that reproduce the patient's known ischemic pattern
Use lead II alone regardless of prior changes
Choose leads only according to surgical site
Avoid ST trending because baseline abnormalities invalidate monitoring
questions.explanation: Fingerprinting selects leads that match the patient's known preop ECG changes.

questions.stem: A high-risk CAD patient is monitored only in lead II throughout major vascular surgery. What is the principal limitation?
options: Ischemia occurring in territories poorly represented by lead II may go undetected
Lead II always overdiagnoses ST depression
Lead II prevents automated ST analysis
questions.explanation: A single lead misses ischemia that multiple leads would detect.

questions.stem: Compared with a 3-cable system, how many ECG views does a 5-cable system provide?
questions.explanation: A 5-cable system provides six views; a 3-cable system provides two.

questions.stem: Five electrodes are placed in nonstandard positions to derive a 12-lead ECG during chest surgery. Which system is being used?
questions.explanation: EASI derives a 12-lead ECG from unconventional electrode placement.

questions.stem: Which FIVE steps should be completed before induction to optimize ECG monitoring? (Select 5)
options: Use only one lead for simplicity
questions.explanation: Print a baseline, optimize waveform size, turn ST monitoring on, and verify placement.

questions.stem: Immediately after electrode placement, lead II unexpectedly shows inverted P waves in a patient whose preoperative tracing had upright P waves. What should be checked FIRST?
options: Treat immediately for ectopic atrial rhythm
Switch to V5 without checking electrodes
questions.explanation: "Trust but verify" means checking electrode placement even when others applied them.

questions.stem: The usual precordial electrode location overlaps the sterile thoracotomy field. Which adjustment BEST preserves monitoring?
options: Relocate electrodes outside the field while maintaining an appropriate lead vector
Remove ECG monitoring during the thoracic portion
Place the electrode beneath the sterile field
Use pulse oximetry in place of ECG
questions.explanation: Surgical site and position may require moving electrodes away from the field.

questions.stem: For anterior-wall ischemia surveillance, which THREE precordial leads provide the best coverage? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Preferred ischemia leads are V3 (most sensitive), V4, V5, III, and aVF.

questions.stem: A patient has a characteristic preoperative ischemic ST pattern in leads III and aVF. Which intraoperative approach BEST uses that baseline information?
options: Include III and aVF in surveillance so new deviation can be compared with the patient's known pattern
Avoid those leads because baseline abnormalities make them unusable
Use lead II alone because inferior leads add no information
questions.explanation: Fingerprinting prioritizes leads with baseline changes.

questions.stem: At the end of anesthesia, ECG electrodes are disconnected for transfer while the patient is still in the OR and anesthesia care is ongoing. Which requirement is no longer met?
options: Continuous ECG display through the period before leaving the anesthetizing location
ECG display only during surgical stimulation
ECG monitoring only for patients with cardiac disease
questions.explanation: ASA requires continuous ECG display from the start of anesthesia until leaving the room.

questions.stem: If V3 is most sensitive for ischemia in the cited study, which lead was second most sensitive?
questions.explanation: Landesberg found V3 most sensitive (86.8%), then V4 (78.9%), then V5 (65.8%).

questions.stem: During vascular surgery, a patient develops a new horizontal ST-segment depression without QRS widening or electrolyte abnormalities. Which perioperative process should be considered?
questions.explanation: Most ischemic events show ST depression.

questions.stem: An adult's mid-arm circumference is 35 cm. Which cuff bladder dimensions most closely match standard sizing principles?
options: Width about 14 cm and length about 28 cm
Width about 7 cm and length about 18 cm
Width about 21 cm and length about 35 cm
Width about 28 cm and length about 14 cm
questions.explanation: A correct cuff has a bladder width of 40% and length of 80% of arm circumference.

questions.stem: NIBP repeatedly reads 178/96 mmHg while a well-leveled arterial line reads 145/82 mmHg. The cuff bladder is visibly too narrow for the arm. Which explanation is MOST likely?
options: An undersized cuff requires excessive pressure to occlude the artery and reads falsely high
An undersized cuff reads falsely low
The discrepancy proves the arterial line is overdamped
Cuff size affects diastolic but not systolic pressure
questions.explanation: An undersized cuff needs higher pressure to occlude the artery, falsely raising the reading.

questions.stem: A very large thigh cuff is used on a thin upper arm and reads substantially below a simultaneous appropriately sized cuff. Which mechanism BEST explains the bias?
options: The oversized bladder occludes the artery at a lower cuff pressure, producing a falsely low reading
Oversized cuffs systematically read falsely high
The thin arm must be positioned below the heart
Large cuffs affect only pulse pressure
questions.explanation: An oversized cuff occludes the artery at lower pressure, falsely lowering the reading.

questions.stem: A patient's NIBP cuff is 20 cm below the level of the right atrium. Compared with a heart-level measurement, what direction of error is expected?
options: Falsely high because of the hydrostatic pressure column
Falsely low because of the hydrostatic pressure column
questions.explanation: A limb below the heart gives falsely high readings.

questions.stem: A patient's NIBP cuff is positioned well above the level of the right atrium during lateral surgery. Compared with a heart-level measurement, what bias is expected?
questions.explanation: A limb above the heart gives falsely low readings.

questions.stem: Compared with upper-arm measurements, what bias is common with forearm NIBP?
questions.explanation: Forearm measurements can overestimate BP.

questions.stem: An NIBP cuff cycles every minute on the same arm for 6 hours. Which THREE complications can result? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Repeated cuff cycling can cause nerve injury, compartment syndrome, and IV interference.

questions.stem: A functioning peripheral IV is infusing vasoactive medication in the right arm and both upper limbs are otherwise usable. Where should the routine NIBP cuff preferentially be placed?
options: On the contralateral arm to avoid repeated interruption of the infusion
On the same arm so both therapies are monitored together
Over the IV site to detect infiltration
On the forearm of the IV arm regardless of cuff fit
questions.explanation: Use the contralateral limb to avoid IV interference.

questions.stem: Which FOUR limb conditions should generally be avoided for routine NIBP cuff placement? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Avoid repeated cuff occlusion over fractures, open injuries, fistulas, or PICC lines.

questions.stem: A patient has prior axillary lymph-node dissection with chronic ipsilateral arm edema. Why is repeated NIBP cycling on that arm undesirable when another site is available?
options: Repeated compression may worsen edema and contribute to skin or nerve injury
The cuff will always read falsely low but causes no tissue risk
It commonly ruptures the brachial artery
questions.explanation: Repeated cuff inflation can worsen edema and cause injury.

questions.stem: During oscillometric NIBP measurement, the monitor directly identifies one pressure from the point of maximal cuff-pressure oscillations and algorithmically derives the others. Which pressure is most directly measured?
questions.explanation: MAP corresponds to maximal oscillation amplitude; systolic and diastolic are derived by algorithm.

questions.stem: A patient has NIBP 150/90 mmHg with a regular rhythm. Using the common approximation, what is the MAP?
questions.explanation: MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 90 + 60/3 = 110 mmHg.

questions.stem: During severe hypotension, Korotkoff sounds are difficult to hear. While slowly deflating the cuff, the radial pulse first reappears at 85 mmHg. What does this palpated value approximate?
questions.explanation: Palpation estimates systolic pressure as the pulse returns during deflation.

questions.stem: During manual BP measurement, Korotkoff sounds first appear at 140 mmHg and disappear at 85 mmHg. How should the measurement be recorded?
options: Systolic 140 mmHg with no estimate of diastolic pressure
questions.explanation: Korotkoff sounds estimate systolic pressure when they appear and diastolic when they disappear.

questions.stem: During induction, NIBP cycles every 5 minutes while pressure is changing rapidly after propofol and vasopressor dosing. Why may this interval be inadequate even though it meets the routine minimum?
options: Intermittent measurements more than about 3 minutes apart may poorly represent rapidly changing hemodynamics
Oscillometric devices become inaccurate whenever vasopressors are used
Five-minute cycling is prohibited during induction
Only invasive pressure can be used after propofol
questions.explanation: The chapter suggests usefulness declines when intervals exceed about 3 minutes.

questions.stem: A premature infant with a patent ductus arteriosus has different upper- and lower-extremity pressures. Which cuff location best reflects pressure delivered to the cerebral circulation?
options: Right arm because it is preductal
Left leg because it is postductal
All limbs are equivalent in a PDA
questions.explanation: The right arm is preductal, reflecting blood that perfuses the brain.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors can make oscillometric NIBP less reliable? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Low flow, stiffness, motion, arrhythmia, leaks, and rapid deflation impair reliability.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with hypertension becomes hypotensive immediately after induction. Which NIBP strategy best captures the evolving response to treatment?
options: Cycle more frequently, potentially every 1–3 minutes during the unstable period
Maintain 5-minute cycling because shorter intervals add no information
Extend to 10 minutes to reduce cuff injury
questions.explanation: More frequent BP measurement is recommended during induction because induction agents cause rapid changes.

questions.stem: A stable anesthetized patient has NIBP programmed every 7 minutes because continuous ECG and pulse oximetry are normal. Which change is required?
options: Shorten the interval so arterial pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every 5 minutes
No change is needed in a stable patient
Extend the interval to 10 minutes once incision is complete
Use 7-minute intervals unless vasoactive medication is administered
questions.explanation: BP must be recorded at least every 5 minutes.

questions.stem: A patient with severe coronary disease has large BP swings during induction. Why should pressure often be assessed more frequently than the routine 5-minute minimum?
options: Brief hypotension or hypertension may create clinically important myocardial supply-demand imbalance between intermittent readings
Coronary disease makes oscillometric cuffs inherently inaccurate
Every patient with coronary disease requires an arterial catheter
Frequent cycling prevents myocardial ischemia regardless of BP
questions.explanation: Limited reserve and IHD warrant closer monitoring.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 52 has a short, conical upper arm and repeated inconsistent NIBP values. Which correction is most appropriate before assuming true hemodynamic instability?
options: Use a cuff/site that provides appropriate bladder dimensions and fit for the arm geometry
Use a smaller cuff so it remains tightly secured
Place the same cuff more distally regardless of fit
Average the inconsistent readings without changing technique
questions.explanation: Arm size and shape change cuff fit, so an appropriately sized cuff or alternative site is needed.

questions.stem: Both upper extremities are unavailable because of dialysis fistulas and positioning. What is the best alternative NIBP site?
options: On the forearm over an IV
Nowhere, so BP is not measured
questions.explanation: The lower extremity is an alternative when the upper arms are unavailable.

questions.stem: NIBP reads 180/100 mmHg using a visibly undersized cuff. Before treating severe hypertension, how should the value be interpreted?
options: The true pressure may be substantially lower because an undersized cuff reads falsely high
The true pressure is probably higher because small cuffs read low
Cuff size changes only diastolic pressure
The displayed value is reliable if the patient is motionless
questions.explanation: A small cuff overestimates BP.

questions.stem: In lateral position, the NIBP cuff is elevated well above the right atrium and reads 90/50 mmHg. What should be considered before giving a vasopressor?
options: Hydrostatic error may make the true heart-level pressure higher than displayed
The true pressure is probably even lower
Correct cuff sizing eliminates height-related error
A cuff above the heart reads falsely high
questions.explanation: Limb above heart level produces falsely low readings.

questions.stem: An oscillometric monitor reports SBP 122, MAP 79, and DBP 61 mmHg. Which value is derived most directly from the oscillation envelope rather than estimated by device-specific algorithms?
questions.explanation: SBP and DBP are estimated using device-specific algorithms.

questions.stem: A patient with prior TIA undergoes carotid endarterectomy with expected clamp-related cerebral perfusion changes and tight beat-to-beat pressure goals. Which additional monitoring combination is most defensible beyond standard monitors?
options: Arterial pressure monitoring plus cerebral monitoring such as cerebral oximetry and/or processed EEG as clinically appropriate
Holter monitoring, treadmill testing, and home glucose monitoring
Pulse oximetry plus intermittent NIBP only
