questions.explanation: Additional monitors include cerebral oximetry, BIS, invasive pressure, precordial stethoscope, TEE, and ICP monitoring as indicated.

questions.stem: During carotid cross-clamping, systemic SpO2 remains 100% while concern arises for ipsilateral cerebral hypoperfusion. Which additional monitor is designed to detect regional cerebral oxygenation change?
questions.explanation: Cerebral oximetry is used in carotid surgery to detect reduced cerebral oxygenation.

questions.stem: During sitting craniotomy, ETCO2 abruptly falls and a characteristic churning sound is heard over the precordium. What complication should be suspected?
questions.explanation: A precordial stethoscope can detect the mill-wheel murmur of air embolism, a form of PE.

questions.stem: Processed EEG will be used to trend hypnotic effect during GA. Why should a value be obtained before induction?
options: It establishes the patient's awake reference for interpreting subsequent changes
The preinduction value predicts exact MAC requirement
Processed EEG cannot function after neuromuscular blockade unless calibrated awake
The baseline replaces clinical assessment of anesthetic depth
questions.explanation: A BIS baseline should be obtained before induction to interpret later values.

questions.stem: A calm 8-year-old is scheduled for mask induction. When should standard monitors ideally be applied if tolerated?
options: While the child is awake, if tolerated
After induction, to avoid upsetting the child
Pulse oximetry alone until the IV is placed
questions.explanation: Starting monitors while the child is awake provides baseline values, when the child tolerates it.

questions.stem: A patient is placed in beach-chair position. The arterial catheter is in the radial artery, but the transducer remains attached near hip level. What is the immediate technical concern?
options: The displayed pressure will be hydrostatically distorted unless the transducer is leveled to the chosen reference point
The catheter must be moved to the femoral artery
Radial arterial pressure cannot be monitored in beach-chair position
The transducer must always be placed at the arterial catheter insertion site
questions.explanation: Transducers are zeroed and leveled at the right atrium; errors in height change the displayed pressure.

questions.stem: An arterial-line MAP suddenly falls from 75 to 45 mmHg, but the patient appears unchanged and NIBP is 74 mmHg. What should be done before giving a vasopressor?
options: Verify transducer level/zero, tubing and catheter patency, and waveform fidelity
Treat the arterial value because invasive pressure always overrides NIBP
Ignore the arterial line and remove it
Increase flush pressure until the MAP matches NIBP
questions.explanation: Verify leveling, tubing, catheter patency, and waveform fidelity before treating.

questions.stem: Which artery is most commonly chosen for routine invasive arterial pressure monitoring?
questions.explanation: The radial artery is the most common site for arterial cannulation.

questions.stem: A normal Allen test is documented before radial cannulation. Which conclusion is justified?
options: It does not reliably guarantee freedom from ischemic complications
It proves collateral circulation is adequate
It eliminates the need to assess the hand after cannulation
It is more reliable than ultrasound for predicting ischemia
questions.explanation: The Allen test has not been confirmed as a reliable predictor of ischemic complications.

questions.stem: A profoundly hypotensive patient has a barely palpable radial pulse and small-caliber vessel. Which technique is most likely to improve first-pass arterial cannulation success?
options: Repeated blind palpation because ultrasound is less useful in low flow
Waiting for a strong pulse before attempting access
questions.explanation: Ultrasound improves success when pulses are weak or vessels small.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing major vascular surgery is expected to have abrupt pressure changes and requires continuous norepinephrine titration. Which monitoring choice best fits both needs?
options: Place an arterial catheter for beat-to-beat pressure and titration
Use pulse oximeter plethysmography as the primary pressure monitor
Use manual palpation after each norepinephrine change
questions.explanation: Arterial lines are indicated for expected rapid BP changes and vasoactive titration, as well as frequent labs and respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings are contraindications to arterial cannulation at a proposed site? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Compromised collateral flow, local infection, or proximal injury/thrombosis prevent accurate readings.

questions.stem: An arterial line reads 168/60 mmHg while NIBP is 140/64; the MAPs are nearly identical. Fast-flush testing produces multiple oscillations. Which interpretation is best?
options: The arterial system is underdamped, exaggerating systolic pressure while MAP remains relatively reliable
The system is overdamped, exaggerating systolic pressure
The NIBP cuff must be undersized
The arterial transducer is necessarily too high
questions.explanation: Underdamping causes systolic overshoot of about 15–30 mmHg, while MAP remains accurate.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform becomes rounded with loss of the dicrotic notch; invasive SBP is 20 mmHg below NIBP while MAPs remain similar. Which technical problem is most likely?
options: Overdamping from causes such as air, clot, or kinking
questions.explanation: Overdamping from air, clot, or kinks blunts the trace and underestimates systolic.

questions.stem: Which THREE system features commonly degrade arterial waveform fidelity? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Air bubbles, long tubing, stopcocks, clots, and kinks degrade fidelity.

questions.stem: After a fast flush is released, the arterial trace oscillates once or twice and rapidly returns to baseline. What does this response indicate?
options: Appropriate dynamic response with near-optimal damping
questions.explanation: Optimal damping shows one or two oscillations before returning to baseline.

questions.stem: After fast-flush release, the arterial waveform rings through many oscillations before settling. What error is most likely in the displayed pressure?
options: Optimal damping with accurate systolic pressure
questions.explanation: Multiple oscillations after a fast flush indicate an underdamped system.

questions.stem: After fast-flush release, the trace returns slowly to baseline with essentially no oscillation. The arterial waveform is blunted. Which condition is present?
questions.explanation: A slow return without oscillations indicates overdamping, often from air or clot.

questions.stem: An arterial system is confirmed to be underdamped. Which displayed component is most likely to mislead the clinician if interpreted without considering waveform fidelity?
options: A falsely low MAP in every case
A falsely high diastolic pressure with normal systolic
questions.explanation: Underdamped systems overestimate SBP.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform is sluggish and the fast-flush test shows no oscillations. Which correctable system problem should be sought first?
options: Air bubbles, clot, kinking, or excessive compliance causing overdamping
A transducer positioned slightly below the atrium
questions.explanation: Overdamping often comes from air bubbles or clot.

questions.stem: Two arterial systems are leveled correctly, but one reproduces the arterial waveform poorly despite a patent catheter. Which dynamic characteristics should be evaluated with a fast-flush test?
options: Catheter insertion angle and arm circumference
questions.explanation: The fast-flush test estimates damping coefficient and natural frequency of the system.

questions.stem: Despite correct leveling, an arterial waveform remains inaccurate. Which properties determine dynamic fidelity?
questions.explanation: Dynamic fidelity depends on damping and natural frequency.

questions.stem: On an arterial waveform, the dicrotic notch appears immediately after the systolic downslope begins. Which cardiac event produces it?
questions.explanation: The dicrotic notch marks aortic valve closure.

questions.stem: On an arterial waveform, what does the lowest point immediately before the next systolic upstroke represent?
questions.explanation: The lowest point is the DBP.

questions.stem: The monitor reports MAP 84 mmHg while the simple DBP + 1/3 pulse-pressure formula gives 81 mmHg. Why can the values differ?
options: The monitor integrates the arterial pressure waveform over the cardiac cycle rather than using the bedside approximation
The monitor calculates MAP from systolic pressure alone
The formula is valid only for invasive pressure
The monitor uses pulse-oximeter timing to calculate MAP
questions.explanation: The monitor calculates MAP as the average pressure from the area under the curve.

questions.stem: If invasive arterial pressure is 160/60 mmHg, what is the pulse pressure?
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic = 160 − 60 = 100 mmHg.

questions.stem: Simultaneous radial and dorsalis-pedis arterial lines show nearly identical MAPs, but pedal SBP is 20 mmHg higher. Which physiologic phenomenon best explains the pattern?
options: Hydrostatic error necessarily caused by the pedal transducer
questions.explanation: Systolic pressure rises as the pulse travels peripherally because of wave reflection; MAP stays similar.

questions.stem: In severe peripheral vascular disease with markedly different limb pressures, which extremity pressure should guide management?
questions.explanation: Use the greater value in severe PVD.

questions.stem: A small air bubble remains in pressurized arterial-line tubing. Why must it be removed before activating a rapid flush?
options: The flush can force air into the arterial circulation and cause embolic injury
Air causes only waveform overdamping and no patient risk
Pressurized flushes draw air away from the patient
Arterial air cannot embolize because arterial pressure is positive
questions.explanation: Pressurized flush systems can push air into the artery, causing embolism.

questions.stem: A neonate receives a continuous arterial-line flush at 3–6 mL/hr. Why does this routine adult-style setup require special attention?
options: It can deliver roughly 72–144 mL/day, a clinically important fluid load for a neonate
The flush volume is negligible below 10 mL/hr
Neonates require higher flush rates to prevent thrombosis
The flush affects only waveform fidelity, not fluid balance
questions.explanation: At 3–6 mL/hr, a continuous flush adds about 72–144 mL per day, which is significant for a neonate.

questions.stem: A radial arterial catheter has been in place for several days. Which FOUR complications should be monitored for? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Arterial line complications include hematoma, thrombosis, ischemia, embolism, infection, nerve injury, hemorrhage, and air embolism.

questions.stem: Which THREE arterial cannulation sites are commonly used in pediatric patients? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Common pediatric sites include umbilical, radial, and femoral.

questions.stem: Which complications are particularly associated with umbilical arterial catheters in neonates?
questions.explanation: Umbilical artery catheters carry risks of aortic thrombosis and coarctation.

questions.stem: An arterial pressure setup contains 2 meters of compliant tubing and several stopcocks, and the waveform is distorted. Which modification best improves dynamic fidelity?
options: Shorten the tubing and remove unnecessary stopcocks using stiff, noncompliant tubing
Add another stopcock to damp artifact
questions.explanation: Minimal tubing length and few stopcocks improve arterial line fidelity.

questions.stem: An arterial transducer is accidentally lowered 10 cm below the reference level while the patient remains unchanged. What happens to the displayed pressure?
options: It becomes falsely high because the hydrostatic column adds pressure
It remains unchanged because the catheter is still intravascular
questions.explanation: A transducer below RA level reads falsely high due to hydrostatic pressure.

questions.stem: An arterial transducer is raised substantially above its reference level while the patient's hemodynamics remain unchanged. What happens to the displayed pressure?
options: It remains accurate if zeroing was performed earlier
questions.explanation: Raising the transducer above RA level lowers readings.

questions.stem: During cardiopulmonary bypass recovery, radial arterial pressure is lower than a more central pressure despite correct leveling and waveform fidelity. Which physiologic explanation can account for this?
options: Changes in peripheral/hand vascular resistance can create a radial-to-central pressure gradient
Peripheral wave reflection always makes radial MAP higher than central MAP
Correctly leveled radial pressure must equal central systolic pressure
Stiff monitoring tubing causes a true physiologic pressure gradient
questions.explanation: Hand vascular resistance changes can make radial pressures underestimate central pressures.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter alternates red and infrared light through tissue to estimate arterial saturation. Which wavelength pair is used by a conventional two-wavelength device?
options: Approximately 660 nm red and 940 nm infrared
questions.explanation: Pulse oximeters use 660 nm (red) and 940 nm (infrared) light.

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry estimates relative concentrations of oxyhemoglobin and deoxyhemoglobin from wavelength-dependent light absorption through tissue. Which physical relationship underlies this measurement?
questions.explanation: The Beer-Lambert law relates light absorption to concentration and path length.

questions.stem: A pulse-oximeter probe transmits light through a finger containing arterial blood, venous blood, bone, and soft tissue. How does the device preferentially identify the arterial component?
options: It analyzes the pulsatile change in light absorption with each heartbeat
It separately measures venous saturation and subtracts it
It uses a third wavelength specific to arterial hemoglobin
It directly measures arterial blood flow
questions.explanation: Plethysmography separates the pulsatile arterial component from nonpulsatile tissue and venous signal.

questions.stem: A standard two-wavelength pulse oximeter displays SpO2 96% in a patient without dyshemoglobinemia. Which saturation definition is it reporting?
options: Functional saturation: oxyhemoglobin relative to oxyhemoglobin plus deoxyhemoglobin
Fractional saturation including COHb and MetHb in the denominator
questions.explanation: SpO2 is functional saturation; co-oximetry measures fractional.

questions.stem: After benzocaine exposure, PaO2 is high on 100% oxygen but the pulse oximeter remains near 85%. Which property of methemoglobin explains this characteristic reading?
options: Similar absorption of the two pulse-oximeter wavelengths drives the ratio toward a displayed saturation near 85%
MetHb is interpreted entirely as oxyhemoglobin, driving SpO2 toward 100%
MetHb blocks the plethysmographic pulse signal
MetHb causes true PaO2 to fall to the value corresponding to 85% saturation
questions.explanation: MetHb absorbs red and IR 1:1, driving SpO2 toward ~85%.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient is confused and tachycardic with SpO2 99%. Why can the displayed saturation be dangerously reassuring?
options: Conventional pulse oximetry may interpret carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin and read falsely high
Carbon monoxide prevents the probe from detecting a pulse
Standard pulse oximetry directly measures PaO2 rather than hemoglobin species
questions.explanation: COHb causes falsely high SpO2.

questions.stem: Which TWO conditions shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Hypercapnia, acidosis, and hyperthermia shift the curve right. Fetal hemoglobin, alkalosis, and hypothermia shift it left.

questions.stem: A septic patient is febrile, hypercapnic, and acidotic. How do these conditions alter hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?
options: They shift the dissociation curve right, facilitating oxygen unloading to tissues
They shift the curve left and increase oxygen affinity
They shift the curve right and impair tissue unloading
questions.explanation: Fever and acidosis shift the curve right, decreasing affinity and releasing oxygen to tissues.

questions.stem: An ABG shows PaO2 60 mmHg in a patient without dyshemoglobinemia. Which approximate SpO2 should be expected from the standard oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.explanation: PaO2 60 corresponds to about 90% saturation, near the steep part of the curve.

questions.stem: A patient's PaO2 falls from 100 to 60 mmHg with only a modest saturation change, then falls further below 60 mmHg and SpO2 declines rapidly. What property of the oxyhemoglobin curve explains this?
options: Below the shoulder, the curve becomes steep so small PaO2 decreases produce large saturation losses
The curve becomes flatter below PaO2 60 mmHg
Pulse oximetry stops responding below PaO2 60 mmHg
Hemoglobin affinity becomes fixed once saturation reaches 90%
questions.explanation: Desaturation accelerates on the steep portion.

questions.stem: A well-perfused patient has a stable pulse-oximeter reading of 92%. With typical device accuracy in this range, which statement is most appropriate?
options: The true arterial saturation may reasonably be a few percentage points above or below the displayed value
The true saturation is exactly 92% if the waveform is good
A displayed 92% implies true saturation could routinely be 70%
Pulse oximeter accuracy improves to ±0.1% below 95%
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry accuracy is about ±2–3% between 70% and 100%.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors can significantly degrade pulse-oximeter accuracy? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Motion, low perfusion, hypothermia, dyes, nail polish, ambient light, and cautery impair accuracy.

questions.stem: During deep sedation on supplemental oxygen, respiratory effort ceases but SpO2 remains 99% for several minutes. Which monitoring principle is illustrated?
options: Pulse oximetry can lag behind apnea because supplemental oxygen preserves arterial saturation despite absent ventilation
Pulse oximetry directly detects rising PaCO2
Supplemental oxygen causes pulse oximetry to read falsely high despite normal arterial saturation
questions.explanation: With supplemental oxygen, patients can be apneic for minutes before SpO2 falls.

questions.stem: In pediatric anesthesia, pulse oximetry may detect which ETT-position problem sooner than capnography?
options: Esophageal intubation before CO2 fades from the trace
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is more sensitive than capnography for mainstem intubation in pediatrics.

questions.stem: A septic patient has SpO2 98% but worsening lactate, cool mottled skin, and oliguria. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Normal arterial saturation does not establish adequate global or regional oxygen delivery and utilization
The high SpO2 excludes tissue hypoxia
Pulse oximetry directly measures tissue oxygen extraction
Lactate cannot reflect oxygen-delivery problems when SpO2 is normal
questions.explanation: SpO2 measures arterial saturation, not oxygen delivery to or use by tissues.

questions.stem: After smoke inhalation, standard SpO2 is 99% but carbon-monoxide exposure is suspected. Which test is required to quantify dyshemoglobin species?
questions.explanation: Co-oximeters use multiple wavelengths to distinguish COHb and MetHb.

questions.stem: A patient rescued from an enclosed-space fire has headache, confusion, and SpO2 99%. Which next measurement is most important for evaluating the suspected oxygen-carrying abnormality?
options: Repeat standard pulse oximetry on another finger
questions.explanation: COHb causes falsely high SpO2.

questions.stem: Immediately after IV methylene blue, the pulse oximeter abruptly falls despite unchanged ETCO2, hemodynamics, and clinical appearance. What should be considered before treating true hypoxemia?
options: Optical interference from the dye can transiently distort pulse-oximeter readings
Methylene blue necessarily causes acute arterial desaturation
Methylene blue converts hemoglobin to carboxyhemoglobin
questions.explanation: Dyes impair oximeter accuracy.

questions.stem: Which statement about contraindications to pulse oximetry is correct?
options: It is contraindicated in sickle cell
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry has no clinical contraindications.

questions.stem: During deep hypothermia, the pulse-oximeter waveform disappears while ECG remains stable. Which mechanism most directly limits the device?
options: Peripheral vasoconstriction reduces the pulsatile arterial signal needed for analysis
Cold tissue emits infrared light that overwhelms the probe
Low temperature eliminates arterial pulsatility despite preserved flow
questions.explanation: Extreme hypothermia causes vasoconstriction and poor perfusion, reducing the pulsatile signal.

questions.stem: During a long open operation in a cool OR, the patient is exposed to surrounding walls and equipment without direct contact. Which heat-loss mechanism typically contributes the largest share under anesthesia?
questions.explanation: Radiation is the largest source of heat loss under anesthesia.

questions.stem: During an open abdominal case, approximately 200 g of water evaporates from exposed tissue. Using about 0.58 kcal lost per gram evaporated, what heat loss is attributable to evaporation?
questions.explanation: Evaporation removes about 0.58 kcal per gram of water: 200 × 0.58 = 116 kcal.

questions.stem: Which FOUR sites are appropriate core-temperature measurement locations? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Core sites include bladder, distal esophagus, ear canal, trachea, nasopharynx, rectum, and pulmonary artery.

questions.stem: Core temperature is 36.0 °C and mean skin temperature is 32.0 °C. Using mean body temperature ≈ 0.85(core) + 0.15(skin), what is the approximate value?
During rapid active rewarming, pulmonary-artery temperature rises promptly but rectal temperature changes slowly. How should the discrepancy be interpreted?
options: Rectal temperature can lag behind rapidly changing core temperature
Pulmonary-artery temperature is unreliable during rewarming
Rectal temperature always best represents instantaneous core temperature
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature can lag during rapid changes.

questions.stem: Distal esophageal temperature is 36.5 °C while skin temperature is 33 °C. Which statement best describes whole-body thermal status?
options: Neither value alone equals mean body temperature; core is weighted much more heavily than skin
Skin temperature alone best represents whole-body heat content
Distal esophageal temperature numerically equals mean body temperature
Core and skin should be averaged with equal weighting
questions.explanation: Skin temperature does not adequately represent mean body temperature, which weights core 0.85 and skin 0.15.

questions.stem: During volatile anesthesia, ETCO2 rises rapidly despite increased minute ventilation and heart rate climbs to 130/min, but core temperature is only 37.2 °C. Which interpretation is safest?
options: Malignant hyperthermia remains possible because hypercarbia and tachycardia can precede marked hyperthermia
The normal-range temperature effectively excludes malignant hyperthermia
Rising ETCO2 argues against malignant hyperthermia
Malignant hyperthermia usually begins with high fever before hypercarbia
questions.explanation: Hypercarbia and tachycardia are early MH signs; hyperthermia appears late.

questions.stem: At the end of a 6-hour case, core temperature is 34.9 °C. Which FOUR complications should be anticipated? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Hypothermia raises oxygen consumption, impairs coagulation, slows drug metabolism, and increases infection and ischemia risk.

questions.stem: A lightly sedated, awake patient undergoes a 30-minute hand procedure under regional anesthesia and maintains normal thermoregulatory responses. Why may continuous core-temperature monitoring add little in this specific setting?
options: Short duration and preserved thermoregulation make a clinically significant temperature change less likely
Temperature monitoring is contraindicated during regional anesthesia
Skin temperature is always sufficient during sedation
Temperature is never relevant in awake patients
questions.explanation: Continuous temperature monitoring is often uninformative in conscious patients with intact thermoregulation.

questions.stem: During a cardiac case with a pulmonary-artery catheter, which site provides the best direct estimate of core temperature?
questions.explanation: PA blood temperature is a strong core temperature estimate.

questions.stem: Both a patient under general anesthesia and one under neuraxial anesthesia develop perioperative hypothermia. Which shared mechanism contributes?
options: Both can impair afferent/efferent thermoregulatory control and alter vasoconstriction thresholds
Only general anesthesia affects thermoregulation; neuraxial anesthesia cannot
Both increase the vasoconstriction threshold above normal
Neuraxial anesthesia increases central heat production enough to cause redistribution
questions.explanation: Both general and regional anesthesia impair afferent and efferent thermoregulatory control.

questions.stem: Heat is lost to cool walls, the operating table, and moving air. Which THREE mechanisms are involved? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: Heat is lost by radiation (the largest), conduction, convection, and evaporation.

questions.stem: During active rewarming after cardiopulmonary bypass, nasopharyngeal and rectal temperatures differ substantially. Why can monitoring more than one site be useful?
options: Temperature compartments equilibrate at different rates during rapid thermal change
All core sites should be identical at every moment
Pulmonary-artery temperature lags behind peripheral sites during rewarming
questions.explanation: During cooling or rewarming, sites change at different rates.

questions.stem: A short anesthetic is expected to cause little thermal disturbance, whereas another case involves deliberate cooling and rewarming. Which principle determines the need for temperature monitoring?
options: Monitor when clinically significant temperature changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected rather than using duration alone
Temperature monitoring is required only in cardiac surgery
Only pediatric patients require temperature monitoring
Temperature monitoring begins only after malignant hyperthermia is suspected
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring is required when significant temperature changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected.

questions.stem: After intubation, ETCO2 values fall 34 → 22 → 9 → 0 mmHg over four breaths while SpO2 remains 98%. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
options: Esophageal intubation with transient washout of swallowed/gastric CO2
Stable tracheal intubation with sampling delay
questions.explanation: CO2 that fades over a few breaths after intubation is esophageal until proven otherwise; SpO2 lags.

questions.stem: Immediately after CO2 pneumoperitoneum, PIP and plateau pressure both rise while ETCO2 gradually increases. Which mechanism BEST explains the combined pattern?
options: Reduced respiratory compliance plus systemic absorption of insufflated CO2
Isolated bronchospasm plus decreased CO2 production
Malignant hyperthermia causing both airway resistance and rigidity
questions.explanation: Both pressures rose together (compliance), and ETCO2 rose gradually from CO2 absorption.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, low exhaled tidal volume, low PIP, and low ETCO2 alarms occur simultaneously. Which problem should be checked first?
questions.explanation: The three disconnect alarms firing together point to disconnection.

questions.stem: A small cuff leak develops before any alarm threshold is crossed. Which THREE subtle trends may appear first? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: A small leak causes subtle drops in PIP, exhaled volume, and ETCO2 before thresholds.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, inspired CO2 rises to 7 mmHg. While identifying whether absorbent exhaustion or valve dysfunction is responsible, what immediate maneuver reduces rebreathing?
questions.explanation: Inspired CO2 means rebreathing; higher FGF compensates while you check absorbent and valves.

questions.stem: A COPD patient has ETCO2 45 mmHg, PaCO2 58 mmHg, and an obstructive capnogram. Which mechanism best explains the 13-mmHg arterial-to-end-tidal gradient?
options: Increased dead space and V/Q heterogeneity from obstructive lung disease
Sampling-line dilution as the necessary cause
questions.explanation: Obstruction and V/Q mismatch widen the ETCO2–PaCO2 gradient.

questions.stem: During hip arthroplasty, ETCO2 abruptly falls with a preserved waveform at the same time profound hypotension develops. Ventilator settings are unchanged. Which mechanism should be suspected?
options: Reduced pulmonary perfusion, including an embolic event
questions.explanation: A sudden fall with the waveform present and hypotension points to reduced perfusion.

questions.stem: FiO2, ETCO2, and measured anesthetic-agent concentration all abruptly fall near zero, yet chest excursion, SpO2, and hemodynamics remain unchanged. What is most likely?
options: A common gas-sampling line disconnection or occlusion
questions.explanation: When all gases fall together while the patient looks well, the sampling line is the likely problem.

questions.stem: During stable ventilation, ETCO2 alone rises from 38 to 55 mmHg while FiO2 and measured anesthetic-agent concentrations remain stable. Which category should be investigated first?
questions.explanation: A single gas changing points to the patient: hypoventilation, rising CO2 production, or absorption.

questions.stem: During controlled ventilation, a notch appears in every alveolar plateau and the surgeon reports increasing abdominal tone long after the last rocuronium dose. What should be assessed next?
options: Quantitative neuromuscular blockade and the need for additional relaxation
questions.explanation: A curare cleft plus poor relaxation suggests returning muscle activity.

questions.stem: Small regular oscillations on the capnogram match the heart rate. What are they?
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic oscillations reflect heart and great vessel movement.

questions.stem: FiO2 is confirmed at 0.50, yet SpO2 is 88% and PaO2 is 55 mmHg. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Adequate inspired oxygen delivery does not guarantee adequate arterial oxygenation when shunt or V/Q mismatch is present
The oxygen analyzer must be miscalibrated
Pulse oximetry is inherently inaccurate at FiO2 0.50
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 does not measure PaO2; shunt or V/Q mismatch can cause hypoxemia.

questions.stem: During machine checkout, a galvanic O2 sensor reads 18% while exposed to room air. Which action is appropriate before clinical use?
options: Recalibrate it to the expected room-air value or replace the sensor if calibration fails
Proceed because 18% is sufficiently close to 21%
questions.explanation: Galvanic sensors should read 21% on room air; recalibrate or replace.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, inspired O2 falls from 50% to 32% despite unchanged flowmeter settings and no pipeline problem. Which mechanism should be considered?
options: Patient oxygen consumption becomes a substantial fraction of delivered fresh oxygen at low flow
The volatile vaporizer chemically consumes oxygen
The CO2 absorbent consumes enough oxygen to explain the decline
Oxygen analyzers cannot function at low fresh-gas flow
questions.explanation: At low flows, patient O2 consumption can lower FiO2.

questions.stem: During pediatric airway laser surgery, FiO2 remains 0.90 despite adequate oxygenation at lower concentrations. What avoidable hazard is increased most directly?
options: Airway fire from an oxygen-enriched environment
Retinopathy of prematurity in every pediatric patient
questions.explanation: The lecture notes fire risk during pediatric airway surgery; minimize FiO2.

questions.stem: A patient rescued from an enclosed-space fire is confused and tachycardic, but SpO2 is 100%. Which diagnosis remains important despite the reassuring pulse-oximeter value?
options: Methemoglobinemia as the characteristic cause of a 100% reading
Pulse-oximeter probe failure as the only explanation
questions.explanation: COHb causes falsely high SpO2; co-oximetry is needed.

questions.stem: After topical benzocaine, SpO2 settles near 85% and changes little with 100% oxygen. Which diagnosis best explains this saturation behavior?
questions.explanation: MetHb drives SpO2 toward ~85% and does not correct with oxygen.

questions.stem: During pediatric anesthesia, SpO2 falls after marked head flexion while a persistent ETCO2 waveform remains. Breath sounds are now asymmetric. Which airway problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is more sensitive than capnography for mainstem intubation in pediatrics.

questions.stem: A cold, vasoconstricted patient has an intermittent SpO2 signal while the ECG rate remains stable. What is the best first step to improve measurement reliability?
options: Warm the extremity or move the probe to a better-perfused site
Increase FiO2 until a waveform returns
Use ETCO2 as a substitute for oxygenation monitoring
questions.explanation: Poor perfusion from hypothermia limits pulse oximetry.

questions.stem: During sedation on supplemental oxygen, SpO2 remains 98% while respiratory rate falls and ETCO2 rises from 40 to 58 mmHg. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Alveolar hypoventilation is occurring before oxygen desaturation becomes apparent
Ventilation is adequate because SpO2 is normal
Pulmonary embolism is the most likely cause of the rising ETCO2
The capnograph must be inaccurate because SpO2 is unchanged
questions.explanation: Supplemental O2 keeps SpO2 normal while CO2 rises from hypoventilation.

questions.stem: During MAC with nasal capnography, the ETCO2 waveform disappears while the patient remains awake, talking, and clinically well ventilated. What should be checked first?
options: Sampling position/patency and whether exhaled gas is bypassing the nasal cannula during mouth breathing
Begin resuscitation for absent pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: A talking patient is breathing; sampling problems are likely.

questions.stem: PIP abruptly rises from 20 to 45 cmH2O, plateau pressure is unchanged, and wheezing is present. Which response best addresses the likely mechanical problem?
options: Check the ETT/circuit for obstruction while treating bronchospasm
Increase tidal volume to overcome the resistance
Increase PEEP because compliance has fallen
Reduce FiO2 because oxygen is causing the pressure rise
questions.explanation: PIP up with stable plateau suggests resistance; check tube and treat bronchospasm.

questions.stem: After steep Trendelenburg, the pressure-volume loop shows that more pressure is required to deliver the same volume. Which mechanical change has occurred?
questions.explanation: Trendelenburg and pneumoperitoneum reduce compliance.

questions.stem: A pressure-volume loop no longer closes because measured expiratory volume is consistently less than inspiratory volume. Which problem should be investigated?
questions.explanation: An open loop with lower expiratory volume suggests a leak.

questions.stem: A flow-volume loop develops a scooped expiratory limb with reduced expiratory flow. Which physiology does this represent?
questions.explanation: Reduced expiratory flow and scooping indicate obstruction.

questions.stem: A morbidly obese patient requires high peak and plateau pressures to deliver relatively small tidal volumes, without a large peak-to-plateau gradient. Which pattern best fits?
options: Restrictive mechanics from reduced respiratory-system compliance
Obstructive mechanics from isolated airway resistance
questions.explanation: Obesity creates a restrictive pattern.

questions.stem: During laparoscopy, pneumoperitoneum reduces compliance and ETCO2 gradually rises despite unchanged ventilation. Which adjustment most directly addresses the CO2 trend while lung mechanics are reassessed?
options: Increase minute ventilation while using lung-protective pressures and recruitment/PEEP as appropriate
Decrease minute ventilation to reduce airway pressure
questions.explanation: CO2 absorption and reduced compliance often require higher ventilation.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly falls to zero, but PIP and exhaled tidal volume remain unchanged and hemodynamics are stable. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Massive pulmonary embolism with cardiovascular collapse
questions.explanation: Normal ventilation with no ETCO2 suggests a sampling issue.

questions.stem: A capnogram becomes triangular while PIP, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 all fall. Which problem best explains the combined trend?
questions.explanation: Sloping, triangular waveforms often indicate a leak.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, the capnogram becomes flat and the patient is visibly apneic although SpO2 remains 99% on supplemental oxygen. What is the immediate priority?
options: Open/support the airway and provide ventilation as needed
Increase oxygen flow and wait for desaturation
Replace the sampling line before assessing the patient
questions.explanation: A flat trace with apnea requires immediate airway support.

questions.stem: ETCO2 transiently rises immediately after IV sodium bicarbonate despite unchanged ventilation. Which mechanism best explains the change?
options: Bicarbonate buffering generates additional CO2 for pulmonary elimination
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate causes a transient ETCO2 rise.

questions.stem: During one-lung ventilation, ETCO2 is 25 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 55 mmHg. Which mechanism best explains the widened gradient?
options: Increased V/Q mismatch and alveolar dead space
A normal fixed gradient during one-lung ventilation
questions.explanation: OLV increases dead space and widens the gradient.

questions.stem: During MRI under GA, sidestream capnography shows a delayed, damped waveform and ETCO2 lower than expected. Which setup factor should be considered?
options: The long sampling tubing required by the remote environment can delay and distort the sampled signal
MRI magnetic fields increase patient CO2 production
questions.explanation: Long sampling lines can delay and dilute the capnogram.

questions.stem: During low-flow anesthesia, the inspiratory capnogram baseline rises above zero and the CO2 absorbent is exhausted. Which correction directly addresses the cause?
options: Replace the exhausted absorbent while ensuring adequate fresh-gas flow and valve function
questions.explanation: Color change indicates absorbent exhaustion; replace it.

questions.stem: ETCO2 rises from 38 to 62 mmHg despite increased minute ventilation; tachycardia and increasing temperature follow. Which process should be treated as a major concern?
options: Malignant hyperthermia with markedly increased CO2 production
Simple rebreathing as the only possible cause
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 despite increased ventilation suggests increased CO2 production such as MH.

questions.stem: The inspired-O2 analyzer alarms at 18% during GA. Which action has priority?
options: Immediately ensure delivery of a safe oxygen source/concentration while investigating the cause
Check pipeline pressure before changing gas delivery
Wait for SpO2 to decrease before intervening
questions.explanation: A low inspired O2 alarm requires immediate action to prevent hypoxic delivery.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, which monitor is expected to identify persistent esophageal placement before pulse oximetry typically changes?
options: Capnography showing absent or rapidly disappearing sustained exhaled CO2
questions.explanation: The low ETCO2 alarm detects esophageal intubation immediately, before desaturation.

questions.stem: PIP rises, plateau pressure remains near baseline, bilateral wheezing develops, and the capnogram becomes shark-fin shaped. Which diagnosis best unifies the findings?
questions.explanation: Shark-fin and high PIP with equal sounds suggests bronchospasm.

questions.stem: After patient repositioning, PIP rises abruptly and breath sounds become absent on the left. Which two diagnoses should be rapidly distinguished?
questions.explanation: Unilateral absent sounds suggest pneumothorax or mainstem intubation.

questions.stem: PIP and exhaled tidal volume fall, but a smaller ETCO2 waveform persists. Which circuit problem is most consistent with this pattern?
options: A partial leak that still permits some ventilation
questions.explanation: A leak can lower PIP and exhaled Vt while ETCO2 persists.

questions.stem: Motion artifact repeatedly triggers low-SpO2 alarms during an otherwise stable anesthetic. Which response best preserves safety?
options: Correct the probe/site or source of artifact while keeping clinically appropriate alarms active
Use ETCO2 as the sole oxygenation monitor
questions.explanation: Alarms must remain active and meet standards; fix the cause.

questions.stem: A clinician lowers the SpO2 alarm threshold to 80% solely to suppress nuisance alarms. Why is this unsafe?
options: Alarm customization should remain clinically appropriate and cannot substitute for correcting artifact or assessing the patient
Lower thresholds make the monitor too sensitive
Changing alarm limits alters the actual SpO2 measurement
A lower limit necessarily produces more nuisance alarms
questions.explanation: Changing alarms must still meet standards and protect the patient.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient suffers unrecognized hypoventilation while receiving supplemental oxygen. Which monitoring omission matches the recurrent failure identified in the closed-claims material?
options: Failure to place an arterial catheter
questions.explanation: Every hypoventilation claim involved failure to monitor ventilation.

questions.stem: A capnogram develops a terminal upward deflection near the end of expiration in a patient with inadequate expiratory time and stiff lungs. Which named morphology is this?
questions.explanation: A pigtail suggests poor compliance or breath stacking.

questions.stem: A remote anesthetizing location loses mains power and all non-battery-backed monitors shut down. Which pre-case preparation would most directly reduce this vulnerability?
options: Verify battery-powered backup equipment and adequate battery charge
Open the backup oxygen cylinder regardless of pipeline status
questions.explanation: The note emphasizes spare batteries and battery equipment function.

questions.stem: A high-PEEP alarm activates. Which broad ventilator-alarm category does this belong to?
options: Oxygen analyzer alarms in the inspired limb
questions.explanation: High PEEP is listed among other ventilator alarms.

questions.stem: Compared with normal lungs, an emphysematous lung accepts a given volume at lower distending pressure. What mechanical property does this describe?
questions.explanation: Increased compliance means less pressure for the same volume.

questions.stem: PIP rises abruptly while plateau remains unchanged after the head is repositioned. What quick bedside maneuver can assess whether the ETT lumen is patent?
options: Pass a suction catheter through the ETT
Obtain chest radiography before examining the tube
questions.explanation: A suction catheter rules out kinks and secretions.

questions.stem: Inspired CO2 remains elevated after fresh absorbent is installed. Which circuit causes should be evaluated next?
options: Unidirectional-valve dysfunction and inadequate fresh-gas flow
questions.explanation: Rebreathing can come from faulty valves or insufficient FGF.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 20 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 40 mmHg and a sustained waveform is present. Which physiologic explanation is most likely?
options: Increased alveolar dead space and/or reduced pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: A large gradient suggests dead space or low perfusion.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly falls to 10 mmHg while severe hypotension and bradycardia develop. Which category of problem is most concerning?
options: Critical loss of pulmonary perfusion from impending arrest or a massive embolic event
Simple sampling artifact despite hemodynamic collapse
questions.explanation: Low ETCO2 with hemodynamic collapse suggests severe perfusion failure.

questions.stem: ETCO2 gradually rises with a preserved waveform and unchanged ventilator settings. Which causes belong highest on the initial differential?
options: Reduced alveolar ventilation or increased CO2 production
A sudden increase in dead space from cardiovascular collapse
questions.explanation: A normal shape with rising ETCO2 suggests hypoventilation or increased production.

questions.stem: A patient develops wheezing and a progressively more sloped expiratory upstroke/plateau while PIP rises and plateau pressure remains stable. Which process is worsening?
questions.explanation: Bronchospasm increases airway resistance, producing a rising PIP with relatively unchanged plateau pressure and a progressively sloped shark-fin capnogram.

questions.stem: After prone positioning, the capnogram becomes shark-fin shaped and PIP rises while plateau pressure is unchanged. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Increased airway resistance from bronchospasm or partial ETT obstruction
questions.explanation: High PIP and shark-fin indicate obstruction.

questions.stem: The inspiratory capnogram baseline remains above zero despite adequate fresh-gas flow. Which causes should be investigated?
options: Rebreathing from unidirectional-valve dysfunction or analyzer zero/calibration error
Pulmonary embolism as the characteristic cause of elevated inspired CO2
questions.explanation: Persistent inspired CO2 despite adequate fresh-gas flow suggests rebreathing from unidirectional-valve dysfunction or an analyzer zero/calibration problem.

questions.stem: During cemented arthroplasty, ETCO2 suddenly falls from 36 to 20 mmHg with a preserved waveform and simultaneous hypotension. Which physiologic event is most concerning?
options: Abrupt reduction in pulmonary perfusion from an embolic event
Sampling-line occlusion, which should abolish the waveform
questions.explanation: An abrupt ETCO2 decrease with a preserved waveform plus hypotension during cemented arthroplasty suggests an acute reduction in pulmonary perfusion from an embolic event.

questions.stem: After head rotation, ETCO2 and SpO2 both fall and breath sounds become markedly asymmetric. Which airway problem should be evaluated immediately?
options: Endobronchial migration or partial ETT obstruction associated with repositioning
questions.explanation: Head rotation can migrate or kink the ETT; falling SpO2/ETCO2 with asymmetric breath sounds requires immediate assessment for endobronchial migration or partial obstruction.

questions.stem: SpO2 falls while FiO2 and ETCO2 remain unchanged and ventilation appears adequate. Which problem category should move higher on the differential?
options: An oxygenation problem such as atelectasis, shunt, or V/Q mismatch
Primary hypoventilation as demonstrated by rising ETCO2
questions.explanation: Falling SpO2 with stable FiO2, ETCO2, and ventilation points toward an oxygenation problem such as atelectasis, shunt, or V/Q mismatch.

questions.stem: SpO2 abruptly falls when electrocautery begins, but the pleth waveform simultaneously becomes erratic and the patient otherwise appears unchanged. What is the best first response?
options: Assess the patient and probe signal for electrocautery artifact before accepting the displayed saturation as true
Treat severe hypoxemia based only on the number
questions.explanation: Electrocautery can distort pulse-oximeter signals; assess the patient and pleth waveform before treating an isolated abrupt saturation change as true hypoxemia.

questions.stem: Pulse oximetry becomes unreliable in a severely hypothermic, vasoconstricted patient. What technical limitation is responsible?
options: Loss of an adequate pulsatile peripheral perfusion signal
questions.explanation: Severe hypothermia causes peripheral vasoconstriction and weak pulsatile flow, reducing the signal pulse oximetry requires.

questions.stem: A septic patient has SpO2 100% but worsening lactate, mottling, and oliguria. What limitation of pulse oximetry does this demonstrate?
options: Arterial saturation does not establish adequate tissue oxygen delivery or utilization
A normal SpO2 excludes tissue hypoxia
Pulse oximetry directly measures cardiac output
Lactate is unrelated to perfusion when SpO2 is normal
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry measures arterial hemoglobin saturation, not tissue oxygen delivery or utilization; tissue hypoperfusion can exist despite SpO2 100%.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has SpO2 99% despite headache and confusion. Which measurement is needed to evaluate the suspected dyshemoglobinemia?
questions.explanation: Underdamping overestimates SBP by 15–30 mmHg; MAP is less affected.

questions.stem: After topical benzocaine, SpO2 stabilizes near 85% despite supplemental oxygen and PaO2 is adequate. Which dyshemoglobinemia should be suspected?
options: Sulfhemoglobinemia as the expected benzocaine effect
No dyshemoglobinemia because PaO2 is adequate
questions.explanation: A damped waveform suggests overdamping; troubleshoot the system first.

questions.stem: Immediately after methylene blue administration, SpO2 falls transiently despite unchanged ventilation, hemodynamics, and clinical appearance. How should this be interpreted?
options: The dye can transiently interfere with optical pulse-oximeter measurement
questions.explanation: In severe PVD, use the greater value.

questions.stem: A profoundly anemic patient has SpO2 100% but shows evidence of inadequate oxygen delivery. Why is the saturation alone reassuring only about one component of oxygen content?
options: SpO2 reflects hemoglobin saturation but not the amount of hemoglobin available to carry oxygen
SpO2 directly measures total arterial oxygen content
Anemia causes standard pulse oximeters to report hematocrit
A saturation of 100% guarantees normal oxygen delivery regardless of hemoglobin concentration
questions.explanation: Vasodilators can make radial pressures underestimate central pressures.

questions.stem: Acidosis, hypercapnia, and hyperthermia shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. What is the principal consequence?
options: Lower hemoglobin oxygen affinity with enhanced unloading to tissues
Higher oxygen affinity with impaired unloading
questions.explanation: Umbilical arterial catheters risk aortic thrombosis and other aortic complications.

questions.stem: Alkalosis, hypocapnia, and hypothermia shift the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left. What is the principal consequence?
options: Increased hemoglobin oxygen affinity and reduced tissue unloading
Reduced affinity and increased tissue unloading
Lower arterial saturation at every PaO2
questions.explanation: Continuous flush of 3–6 mL/hr can matter in neonates.

questions.stem: A patient's PaO2 falls to about 60 mmHg and then decreases further. Why can SpO2 now decline rapidly with relatively small additional PaO2 losses?
options: The patient is entering the steep portion of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve
Hemoglobin becomes fully saturated below PaO2 60 mmHg
Pulse oximetry ceases to function below PaO2 60 mmHg
The dissociation curve becomes flatter below this point
questions.explanation: Arterial lines are indicated when vasoactive infusions and rapid BP changes are expected.

questions.stem: A radial arterial catheter is desired, but the proposed wrist has cellulitis while the contralateral site is usable. Which choice best balances monitoring need and procedural risk?
options: Use an alternative uninfected arterial site
Cannulate through the cellulitis and give antibiotics
Proceed if the Allen test is normal
Use the infected arm for NIBP instead
questions.explanation: Local infection is a contraindication to arterial cannulation.

questions.stem: A previously normal radial arterial waveform becomes flat and the catheter no longer flushes, while ECG and pulse oximetry show continued circulation. Which technical problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: A flat, nonflushable line suggests clot or occlusion.

questions.stem: NIBP reads 165/95 mmHg with a visibly undersized cuff on a large arm. Before administering an antihypertensive, what should be done?
options: Repeat the measurement with an appropriately sized cuff
Average the value with the prior reading
Move the same undersized cuff to the forearm
questions.explanation: A small cuff overestimates BP; replace and repeat.

questions.stem: One arm contains a dialysis fistula and the other has an actively infusing IV that should not be repeatedly compressed. Which routine NIBP site is preferable if suitable?
questions.explanation: Avoid cuffs over fistulas; use the lower extremity if arms are unavailable.

questions.stem: A NIBP cuff cycles every minute on the same arm for hours despite stable hemodynamics. Which preventable complication becomes more likely?
options: Compression-related nerve injury or compartment syndrome
Systematic falsely low pressure from repeated inflation
questions.explanation: Frequent cycling can cause nerve injury or compartment syndrome.

questions.stem: Why may 1–3 minute NIBP cycling be appropriate during induction even though the routine minimum interval is longer?
options: Anesthetic and airway interventions can cause rapid pressure changes that would be missed between 5-minute measurements
Oscillometric accuracy improves solely because the cuff cycles faster
Pulse oximetry requires simultaneous rapid cuff cycling
questions.explanation: Induction agents cause cardiac depression and vasodilation.

questions.stem: A premature infant with a patent ductus arteriosus has discrepant limb pressures. Which cuff site best approximates preductal pressure supplying the brain?
questions.explanation: Right-arm preductal pressure best approximates cerebral perfusion.

questions.stem: Oscillometric NIBP values vary widely in atrial fibrillation despite correct cuff size and position. Which feature of the rhythm explains the reduced reliability?
options: Beat-to-beat variation in pulse amplitude and timing complicates oscillation analysis
Atrial fibrillation directly increases cuff pressure
The rhythm always causes falsely high pressure
questions.explanation: Arrhythmia is listed as a factor impairing NIBP reliability.

questions.stem: During vascular surgery, new horizontal ST depression develops in a monitored precordial lead during tachycardia and hypotension. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Treat it as possible myocardial ischemia while correcting supply-demand imbalance and verifying the signal
Dismiss it because ST depression is common under anesthesia
Assume electrode error without checking the patient
Remove the precordial lead and monitor only lead II
questions.explanation: V3 is most sensitive for ischemia; ST depression is typical.

questions.stem: A patient's prior ischemic episodes produced characteristic ST changes in leads III and aVF. How should that information affect intraoperative ECG surveillance?
options: Include leads that reproduce the known pattern while maintaining appropriate rhythm/ischemia monitoring
Avoid III and aVF because baseline abnormalities make them unusable
Use lead II alone regardless of the prior pattern
questions.explanation: Fingerprinting prioritizes leads with baseline changes.

questions.stem: A patient with significant CAD is monitored with only a basic 3-lead configuration. What important limitation remains despite adequate rhythm detection?
options: Reduced sensitivity for detecting ischemia across multiple myocardial territories
Inability to identify any ST change in the displayed lead
questions.explanation: 3-lead systems have limited sensitivity for ischemia.

questions.stem: Immediately after electrode placement, lead II is inverted compared with the patient's known baseline. What should occur before diagnosing a new rhythm or ischemic abnormality?
options: Verify electrode placement and lead configuration
Treat the inversion as myocardial ischemia
Assume it is benign without checking
Switch leads and ignore the discrepancy
questions.explanation: Trust but verify electrode placement.

questions.stem: A preinduction ECG strip is normal, but new ST depression appears after surgical stimulation. What is the principal value of the baseline tracing?
options: It establishes whether the intraoperative change is new
It fulfills all subsequent ischemia assessment
questions.explanation: A baseline strip lets you judge whether intraoperative changes are new.

questions.stem: New ST depression appears with tachycardia and hypotension in a patient with CAD. Which immediate physiologic goal best addresses myocardial oxygen balance?
options: Reduce excessive demand while restoring coronary perfusion pressure and oxygen supply
Deepen anesthesia without assessing pressure or heart rate
Wait for ST elevation before intervening
questions.explanation: Ischemia often presents as ST depression; reduce demand and improve supply.

questions.stem: During GA, distal esophageal temperature is 35.2 °C while exposed-skin temperature is 33 °C. Which value more closely represents core temperature?
options: An equal average of the two
Neither unless a pulmonary-artery catheter is present
questions.explanation: Esophageal is a core site; skin temperature does not represent mean body temperature.

questions.stem: During rapid active rewarming, rectal temperature remains lower than distal esophageal temperature. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Rectal temperature may lag behind rapidly changing central temperature
The esophageal probe is necessarily inaccurate
The patient cannot be rewarming until rectal temperature rises
Rectal temperature always represents the instantaneous central temperature
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature can lag during active cooling or rewarming.

questions.stem: Late in a volatile anesthetic, ETCO2 rises despite increased ventilation, tachycardia develops, and core temperature then begins to increase. Which diagnosis requires immediate consideration?
options: Forced-air warming as the sole explanation
questions.explanation: Temperature rise is a late sign of MH.

questions.stem: A patient reaches 34.5 °C after a long operation. Which pair of effects is most consistent with clinically significant perioperative hypothermia?
options: Impaired coagulation and prolonged drug effects
Reduced infection risk and faster metabolism
Lower oxygen demand during postoperative shivering
questions.explanation: Hypothermia prolongs drug effects and increases bleeding. Shivering raises oxygen demand.

questions.stem: Core temperature falls most rapidly soon after induction even before prolonged environmental exposure. Which mechanism is especially important in this early phase?
options: Anesthetic-induced redistribution of heat from the core to peripheral compartments
Evaporative loss from the lungs as the dominant mechanism
Conductive loss through IV tubing alone
questions.explanation: Anesthesia inhibits thermoregulation; radiation is the largest loss.

questions.stem: During cardiac surgery with a pulmonary-artery catheter, which temperature measurement best reflects core temperature?
options: Skin surface temperature corrected for room temperature
questions.explanation: PA blood temperature is a strong estimate of core temperature.

questions.stem: A lightly sedated patient undergoes a brief hand procedure under regional anesthesia and remains awake with intact thermoregulatory responses. Which statement best describes continuous core-temperature monitoring in this case?
options: It may provide limited additional information when clinically significant temperature change is not expected
It is mandatory solely because any sedation is used
It is contraindicated with regional anesthesia
It is more important than oxygenation monitoring
questions.explanation: In conscious or lightly sedated patients with intact thermoregulation, continuous temperature monitoring may add little.

questions.stem: In lateral position, the NIBP cuff is substantially below the level of the right atrium. How will hydrostatic pressure bias the displayed value?
questions.explanation: Limbs below heart level produce falsely high readings.

questions.stem: In lateral position, the NIBP cuff is on the upper arm substantially above the right atrium. What bias is expected?
questions.explanation: A limb above heart level produces falsely low readings.

questions.stem: The arterial line suddenly reports a much lower SBP, but MAP by NIBP, ETCO2, pulse quality, and the clinical picture are unchanged. What is the best first action?
options: Verify transducer level, catheter/tubing patency, and waveform fidelity before treating
Give a vasopressor based on the invasive SBP
questions.explanation: Verify the line before treating.

questions.stem: A small air bubble enters arterial-pressure tubing and the waveform becomes rounded. Which measurement effect is expected?
options: A higher dicrotic notch with accurate systolic pressure
questions.explanation: Air bubbles increase damping and lower SBP readings.

questions.stem: An arterial line is connected through long compliant tubing with multiple stopcocks. Why can the displayed waveform become misleading?
options: The added compliance and connections degrade the system's dynamic response
Long tubing affects only transducer zero, not waveform fidelity
questions.explanation: Extra tubing and stopcocks degrade fidelity.

questions.stem: Fast-flush release produces one oscillation followed by a crisp arterial waveform with a visible dicrotic notch. How should the dynamic response be interpreted?
questions.explanation: One or two oscillations after flush indicate optimal damping.

questions.stem: In beach-chair position, a radial arterial transducer is leveled at the right atrium and displays MAP 70 mmHg. Why may cerebral arterial pressure be lower?
options: The brain is vertically above the heart, creating a hydrostatic pressure decrease at cerebral level
Upright position makes the heart-level transducer read falsely low
Radial MAP always underestimates cerebral pressure
ETCO2 determines the entire heart-to-brain pressure difference
questions.explanation: Upright positioning means brain pressure is lower than heart-level pressure.

questions.stem: A distal arterial site displays higher systolic pressure and wider pulse pressure than a more central site while MAP is similar. Which phenomenon best explains this?
options: Hydrostatic leveling error in every case
questions.explanation: Peripheral amplification exaggerates SBP and pulse pressure.

questions.stem: A patient requires continuous norepinephrine titration and frequent arterial blood gases during major surgery. Which monitor best serves both purposes?
questions.explanation: Arterial lines allow continuous BP and frequent labs.

questions.stem: Major thoracic surgery with one-lung ventilation is expected to involve rapid hemodynamic changes and repeated blood-gas assessment. Which pressure-monitoring strategy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: OLV and major surgery are indications for invasive BP monitoring.

questions.stem: Simultaneous central and dorsalis-pedis arterial measurements have similar MAPs but higher pedal systolic pressure. Which explanation is most likely?
options: Dorsalis-pedis pressure always underestimates systolic pressure
The pedal transducer must be leveled at the foot
The pedal catheter is measuring venous pressure
questions.explanation: Distal arterial sites show more systolic amplification.

questions.stem: An arterial catheter becomes partially kinked and the waveform is blunted. Which pressure effect is most likely?
options: Overdamping with reduced displayed systolic pressure
Increased systolic pressure with unchanged waveform
questions.explanation: Kinking increases damping.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform develops a slow upstroke, reduced amplitude, and loss of its dicrotic notch while NIBP remains stable. What should be checked first?
options: Overdamping from air, clot, kinking, or excessive tubing
Assume the displayed systolic pressure is accurate
questions.explanation: Delayed, small waveforms suggest overdamping.

questions.stem: The hand distal to a radial arterial catheter becomes cold, pale, and poorly perfused. Which complication requires prompt evaluation?
questions.explanation: Ischemia or thrombosis is a known arterial line complication.

questions.stem: A pressurized arterial-line flush bag empties and the continuous flush stops. Which technical complication becomes more likely over time?
options: Catheter thrombosis/occlusion with loss of waveform
questions.explanation: Without flush, the catheter can clot.

questions.stem: An arterial waveform is damped and a visible air bubble is present in the tubing. Which response is appropriate?
options: Remove the bubble and reassess waveform fidelity before relying on the systolic value
Give a vasopressor to correct the low displayed systolic pressure
Leave the system unchanged because damping never affects interpretation
questions.explanation: Air bubbles cause overdamping and must be removed.

questions.stem: After forceful pressurized flushing of a radial arterial catheter, the hand becomes painful, pale, and poorly perfused. Which complication is most concerning?
options: Arterial injury/thrombosis or embolic compromise causing distal ischemia
A normal transient effect of flushing
Improved perfusion from the pressure wave
questions.explanation: Pressurized flushing can cause air embolism and ischemia.

questions.stem: A patient becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after induction between routine 5-minute NIBP measurements. Which monitoring change would best reduce the chance of missing another rapid episode?
options: Shorten the NIBP cycle during instability or use continuous invasive monitoring when clinically indicated
Add processed EEG instead of pressure monitoring
Use temperature monitoring as a surrogate
questions.explanation: Higher frequency monitoring is recommended during induction.

questions.stem: A patient with limited cardiovascular reserve undergoes major surgery with anticipated rapid blood loss and vasoactive titration. Which BP-monitoring approach is most appropriate?
options: Continuous invasive pressure monitoring or substantially increased measurement frequency based on clinical need
Measure BP only after major surgical events
questions.explanation: Limited reserve warrants increased monitoring frequency.

questions.stem: NIBP reads 88/50 mmHg while the cuffed arm is elevated well above the heart and the patient otherwise appears stable. What should be done before treating the number?
options: Bring the measurement site to the appropriate reference level and repeat the pressure
Accept the reading because cuff height has no effect
questions.explanation: Limb position affects readings; recheck at heart level.

questions.stem: A small cuff on a large arm reads 150/90 mmHg. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The true pressure may be lower because an undersized cuff overestimates BP
The true pressure is probably higher
The reading is unaffected by cuff size
questions.explanation: A small cuff overestimates BP.

questions.stem: During moderate-to-deep propofol sedation for colonoscopy, SpO2, ECG, and NIBP are monitored but exhaled CO2 is not. Which important safety capability is missing?
options: Continuous assessment of ventilation with exhaled CO2 in addition to clinical observation
questions.explanation: Moderate or deep sedation requires qualitative signs plus continuous exhaled CO2.

questions.stem: An awake patient receives an interscalene block without sedation and communicates normally throughout. What ventilation assessment is appropriate under the stated monitoring standard?
options: Continual observation of qualitative clinical signs of ventilation
Mandatory continuous capnography in every unsedated regional anesthetic
questions.explanation: With minimal or no sedation, qualitative clinical signs are required.

questions.stem: During GA, the sole qualified anesthesia professional leaves the room while surgery continues and no qualified replacement assumes care. Which fundamental monitoring principle is violated?
options: Qualified anesthesia personnel must remain present throughout the anesthetic
questions.explanation: Standard I requires qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout the anesthetic.

questions.stem: During otherwise routine anesthesia, NIBP is programmed every 10 minutes. Which minimum circulatory-monitoring requirement is not being met?
options: Arterial pressure and heart rate should be determined/evaluated at least every 5 minutes
Continuous exhaled CO2 is required only every 10 minutes
Temperature must be recorded every 5 minutes
Neuromuscular monitoring substitutes for frequent BP measurement
questions.explanation: BP and HR must be determined at least every 5 minutes.

questions.stem: During mechanical ventilation, the capnography waveform remains displayed but its audible alarm is intentionally silenced for the rest of the case. Why is this unsafe?
options: A displayed respiratory signal does not provide the required audible warning when attention is directed elsewhere
The alarm is needed only during intubation
Silencing the alarm makes ETCO2 numerically inaccurate
Capnography alarms are relevant only during MAC
questions.explanation: When capnography is used, the ETCO2 alarm must be audible.

questions.stem: Mechanical ventilation continues after the breathing-system disconnect alarm is disabled. Which safety layer has been lost?
questions.explanation: A device detecting disconnection with audible alarm is required during mechanical ventilation.

questions.stem: Rocuronium is used and reversal is given without any objective assessment of neuromuscular recovery. Which monitoring problem is most important?
options: Residual neuromuscular blockade may go unrecognized without appropriate neuromuscular monitoring
Inspired-O2 monitoring is unnecessary after reversal
NIBP frequency must be increased solely because reversal was administered
questions.explanation: NMB requires monitoring of depth and recovery.

questions.stem: The workstation functioned normally for an earlier case, so the next anesthetic begins without verifying equipment function. Which safety principle is violated?
options: Anesthesia equipment should be checked for proper function before each anesthetic
A prior successful case substitutes for subsequent checks that day
Only the vaporizer requires rechecking between cases
Equipment verification is required only after a malfunction
questions.explanation: AANA Standard 5 requires equipment verification before each anesthetic.

questions.stem: A cooperative 3-year-old tolerates pulse oximetry before mask induction. Why is obtaining the preinduction value useful?
options: It establishes a baseline against which changes after anesthetic exposure can be interpreted
It eliminates the need for pulse oximetry after induction
It replaces capnography after airway placement
questions.explanation: Applying monitors before induction provides baseline values to compare against later.

questions.stem: A patient with severe obesity has a short, conical upper arm and inconsistent oscillometric pressures. Which technical issue should be corrected before treating the values?
options: Cuff bladder size and fit may be inappropriate for the arm geometry
Adipose tissue makes noninvasive pressure measurement impossible
Oscillometry always reads falsely low in obesity
The cuff should be made as tight and narrow as possible
questions.explanation: Larger arm circumference requires proper cuff selection.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient undergoing GA becomes hypotensive shortly after induction and supine positioning. Why is frequent BP reassessment especially important at this point?
options: Anesthetic vasodilation plus aortocaval compression can produce rapid hemodynamic change
Pregnancy makes all oscillometric measurements inaccurate
General anesthesia in pregnancy always requires an arterial catheter
Frequent cuff cycling prevents aortocaval compression
questions.explanation: Induction agents and positioning can quickly lower BP.

questions.stem: During deep sedation on supplemental oxygen, respiratory rate falls and ETCO2 rises while SpO2 remains 99%. Why would relying on SpO2 alone be dangerous?
options: Supplemental oxygen can delay desaturation despite clinically important hypoventilation
Normal SpO2 proves alveolar ventilation is adequate
Pulse oximetry detects apnea before capnography
questions.explanation: SpO2 is a poor ventilation monitor, especially with supplemental O2.

questions.stem: SpO2 abruptly reads 92% after having been 99%. The provider suspects artifact because the probe has been troublesome. What should occur before dismissing the alarm?
options: Assess the patient and signal quality, then correct the probe if artifact is confirmed
Replace the probe without examining the patient
Assume artifact because prior alarms were false
questions.explanation: Cognitive bias can cause missed hypoxemia; evaluate every alarm.

questions.stem: During an otherwise stable GA, the anesthesia provider repeatedly diverts attention to personal phone use. Which vigilance threat is this?
questions.explanation: Handheld device use is a self-initiated distraction.

questions.stem: A provider is severely sleep-deprived during an overnight emergency case. Which mechanism most directly threatens vigilance?
options: Fatigue and circadian disruption impair sustained attention and judgment
External noise is the primary problem
Equipment failure becomes more common solely because it is nighttime
Sleep deprivation affects documentation but not monitoring
questions.explanation: Human factors include fatigue and circadian disruption.

questions.stem: Loud music prevents the provider from immediately identifying which device generated an alarm. Which human-factors hazard is illustrated?
options: An external auditory distraction interfering with alarm recognition
questions.explanation: Noise and music are external distractions.

questions.stem: During a systematic workstation sweep, the CO2 absorbent is noted to be exhausted before inspired CO2 rises. What is the safety advantage of this check?
options: It identifies a developing rebreathing risk before a physiologic alarm necessarily occurs
questions.explanation: Absorbent color change is part of the machine sweep.

questions.stem: During a long volatile anesthetic, end-tidal agent concentration begins falling despite an unchanged vaporizer dial. Which simple workstation check should be included immediately?
options: Verify vaporizer agent level and delivery
Replace the capnography water trap first
Increase fresh-gas flow without checking the vaporizer
questions.explanation: Vaporizer delivery and fill level are machine sweep items.

questions.stem: Capnography becomes intermittently damped during a humidified case while ventilation remains clinically unchanged. Which workstation component should be inspected early?
options: The water trap and sampling line for condensation or obstruction
questions.explanation: Water trap checks help prevent sampling occlusion.

questions.stem: Hemodynamics and anesthetic depth change unexpectedly after an IV infusion is started. Inspection shows swelling at the catheter site. Which routine patient-sweep item would detect this?
options: Verify that IV access remains patent and noninfiltrated
questions.explanation: The patient sweep includes checking IV function.

questions.stem: A surgical retractor is resting against the patient's face and partially compressing the breathing circuit. Which systematic sweep should detect this hazard?
options: Inspection of the patient/airway and surgical field for equipment pressure or obstruction
questions.explanation: The sweep includes keeping instruments off pressure points and the airway.

questions.stem: Estimated blood loss appears low when only the suction canister is considered, but many saturated sponges are present. Which field-sweep practice prevents this error?
options: Integrate suction volume with laps/sponges and blood elsewhere in the field
Use suction volume alone because it is objective
Estimate blood loss from NIBP trends only
Use ETCO2 as the primary blood-loss monitor
questions.explanation: Blood loss assessment is part of the field sweep.

questions.stem: A long case is approaching a highly stimulating phase followed soon by emergence. Why is tracking surgical progress part of anesthetic vigilance?
options: It allows anticipated changes in stimulation, hemodynamics, ventilation, and anesthetic requirements to be managed proactively
It determines when physiologic monitoring may stop
It allows anesthesia to control the operative schedule
questions.explanation: Tracking the case timeline supports anticipation of upcoming stimulation, hemodynamic changes, and emergence rather than reacting only after they occur.

questions.stem: An ignition source is being used close to oxygen-enriched drapes. Which field-sweep concern takes priority?
options: Recognize and reduce the fire triad risk before activation
Increase FiO2 to shorten the procedure
Ignore the setup if no flame is visible
questions.explanation: The field sweep includes lighted instruments and fire prevention.

questions.stem: A new volatile-agent odor is noticed near the workstation while measured agent concentration begins drifting. Which problem should be investigated?
options: A leak in the breathing system or anesthetic-gas delivery pathway
questions.explanation: Smell can detect volatile leaks.

questions.stem: Immediately after extubation, the monitor values have not yet changed but inspiratory stridor is heard. What does this illustrate?
options: Direct sensory assessment can identify airway obstruction before monitor trends change
Pulse oximetry should always change before airway sounds
Stridor is an expected benign emergence finding
Capnography eliminates the need to listen to the patient
questions.explanation: Hearing identifies abnormal airway sounds like stridor.

questions.stem: A sedated patient shows chest effort but no airflow is felt at the mask. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Respiratory effort does not guarantee effective ventilation; assess and relieve airway obstruction
Capnography is unnecessary when chest movement is visible
questions.explanation: Touch can detect air movement and chest excursion.

questions.stem: During ventilation, condensation appears and disappears synchronously within the clear ETT while chest excursion is present. What can this visual finding contribute?
