options: It is a supportive clinical sign of airflow but does not replace sustained capnographic confirmation
It alone proves correct tube depth
questions.explanation: Sight identifies condensation, chest rise, and skin color.

questions.stem: Sustained exhaled CO2 confirms tracheal ventilation, but left breath sounds are absent after intubation. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Assess ETT depth and exclude right-mainstem intubation while considering other unilateral causes
Accept tube position because capnography is present
Remove the ETT immediately without assessment
Ignore the asymmetry if SpO2 remains normal
questions.explanation: ETCO2 confirms tracheal placement but not endobronchial position.

questions.stem: After head repositioning, ETCO2 remains present but SpO2 falls and breath sounds become asymmetric. Which cause should be checked promptly?
options: Capnography sampling-line obstruction as the sole cause
questions.explanation: Position changes can move the ETT; check placement.

questions.stem: A 4-hour open abdominal operation proceeds without any temperature measurement. Why is this a monitoring deficiency?
options: Clinically significant temperature change is reasonably anticipated during a long open procedure
Temperature monitoring is required only after hypothermia occurs
Open surgery affects skin but not core temperature
Temperature monitoring is unnecessary if forced-air warming is used
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring is required when significant changes are expected.

questions.stem: The oxygen analyzer samples the expiratory rather than inspired limb. Which safety objective is compromised?
options: Early detection of a hypoxic mixture being delivered to the patient
questions.explanation: The O2 sensor should be in the inspired limb to detect hypoxic delivery.

questions.stem: The breathing circuit disconnects while the inspired-O2 analyzer initially continues to display a normal concentration. Why?
options: Fresh gas can still pass the inspired-O2 sensor even though ventilation to the patient is lost
A normal inspired-O2 value proves the patient remains connected
The O2 analyzer directly measures exhaled tidal volume
Circuit disconnection always causes inspired O2 to fall immediately
questions.explanation: Inspired O2 alarms are not reliable disconnect monitors.

questions.stem: PaO2 is 60 mmHg but the pulse oximeter persistently reads 99%. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Investigate the discordance, including dyshemoglobinemia, signal error, and sample/measurement validity rather than assuming either value is correct
Accept the SpO2 because pulse oximetry is always more accurate than ABG
questions.explanation: SpO2 can be falsely high with COHb, or the curve can shift.

questions.stem: PaO2 is approximately 60 mmHg with SpO2 near 90%. Why does further loss of PaO2 become especially concerning?
options: The patient is near the steep portion of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, where saturation can fall rapidly
The curve becomes flatter below this point
Hemoglobin becomes fully saturated at this PaO2
Pulse oximetry stops reflecting saturation below 90%
questions.explanation: PaO2 60 ≈ SpO2 90%, near the steep portion.

questions.stem: Acidosis, hypercapnia, and hyperthermia develop during a case. What happens to hemoglobin-oxygen affinity?
options: It decreases, shifting the curve right and facilitating tissue unloading
It increases, shifting the curve left
questions.explanation: Acidosis and hyperthermia shift the curve right.

questions.stem: SpO2 reaches about 90% and continues falling. Why can subsequent desaturation accelerate?
options: The corresponding PaO2 is entering the steep portion of the dissociation curve
The curve becomes increasingly flat below 90% saturation
questions.explanation: Below ~90%, desaturation can accelerate.

questions.stem: Immediately after injection of a strongly colored intravascular dye, SpO2 falls abruptly while arterial waveform, ETCO2, and clinical appearance remain stable. What should be considered?
options: Transient optical interference with pulse oximetry
Certain true hypoxemia caused by the dye
questions.explanation: Dyes impair pulse oximeter accuracy.

questions.stem: A smoke-inhalation patient has suspected carbon monoxide poisoning despite normal standard SpO2. Which measurement best quantifies the relevant hemoglobin species?
questions.explanation: Co-oximetry distinguishes COHb from oxyhemoglobin.

questions.stem: After benzocaine exposure, SpO2 remains near 85% despite high PaO2. Which optical behavior explains this pattern?
options: Methemoglobin absorbs the two conventional pulse-oximeter wavelengths similarly, driving the ratio toward about 85%
Methemoglobin is read entirely as oxyhemoglobin
Methemoglobin lowers PaO2 in direct proportion to SpO2
The plethysmographic pulse disappears in all methemoglobinemia
questions.explanation: MetHb absorbs red and IR 1:1, driving SpO2 toward 85%.

questions.stem: A pulse-oximeter probe is directly exposed to intense surgical lighting and the displayed value becomes erratic. Which corrective action is appropriate?
options: Shield/reposition the probe and reassess signal quality
Treat the erratic number as definite hypoxemia
Use the same probe without checking because ambient light cannot interfere
questions.explanation: Ambient light can impair pulse oximetry.

questions.stem: Electrocautery produces an apparent wide-complex tachyarrhythmia on ECG, but the arterial waveform and pulse-oximeter pulse rate remain unchanged. What is the best interpretation?
options: ECG artifact is likely; verify the patient's true rhythm using independent pulse/perfusion signals
Treat ventricular tachycardia immediately based only on ECG
The arterial line is necessarily wrong
Pulse signals cannot help distinguish electrical artifact
questions.explanation: Cautery can cause artifact; confirm with another monitor.

questions.stem: New ST depression appears in lead II during hypotension. Which next monitoring step best strengthens the assessment before deciding whether it represents ischemia?
options: Verify signal/electrode quality and examine additional ischemia-sensitive leads while correcting supply-demand abnormalities
Dismiss the change because lead II is primarily a rhythm lead
questions.explanation: Use multiple leads; V3 is most sensitive.

questions.stem: Heart rate is 45/min and the low alarm is set at 40/min. The patient is hemodynamically stable. What is the best approach?
options: Assess the clinical significance and set individualized alarm limits that remain appropriately protective
Lower the limit to 30 solely to avoid future alarms
Ignore the trend because no alarm has sounded
questions.explanation: Alarm limits can be adjusted but must still meet standards.

questions.stem: Multiple alarms activate simultaneously after patient repositioning. What should guide the initial response?
options: Rapid patient assessment while prioritizing threats to oxygenation, ventilation, and circulation and checking for a common cause
Silence every alarm before looking at the patient
Call biomedical engineering before assessing the airway
questions.explanation: Every alarm must be evaluated; prioritize the patient.

questions.stem: Repeated false alarms from a poorly secured probe eventually cause staff to ignore subsequent alarms. Which human-factors problem has developed?
questions.explanation: Alarm fatigue leads to ignoring alarms.

questions.stem: A provider repeatedly scans the patient, airway, IVs, monitors, workstation, and surgical field in a consistent sequence. What is the principal benefit?
options: A systematic sweep reduces omission and helps detect subtle changes before threshold alarms
It guarantees the cause of every abnormality
It eliminates the need for direct patient assessment
questions.explanation: A sweep is a systematic scan of the environment.

questions.stem: PIP, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 drift downward together but remain above alarm thresholds. Which developing problem should be considered?
options: Improving compliance as the only explanation
questions.explanation: Subtle decreases can detect leaks before alarm thresholds.

questions.stem: After intubation, SpO2 remains 100% from preoxygenation but sustained exhaled CO2 is absent. Which monitor provides the earliest routine warning of persistent esophageal placement?
questions.explanation: Capnography detects esophageal intubation earliest.

questions.stem: Alarm limits are widened far beyond clinically appropriate ranges solely to reduce nuisance alerts. What is the major consequence?
options: Important deterioration may progress substantially before an alarm activates
The physiologic measurements become more accurate
questions.explanation: Alarm limits must meet standards to prevent missed events.

questions.stem: In a small child, a precordial stethoscope is used in addition to electronic monitors. What unique continuous information can it provide?
options: Direct heart and breath sounds that may reveal mechanical or airway changes
questions.explanation: Precordial stethoscopes allow continuous auscultation.

questions.stem: During carotid cross-clamping, systemic SpO2 remains normal but concern exists for regional cerebral hypoperfusion. Which monitor can provide regional cerebral oxygenation information?
questions.explanation: Cerebral oximetry detects falling cerebral oxygenation during carotid clamping.

questions.stem: A hypoxic gas mixture reaches the circuit after the workstation check was omitted, despite the machine itself functioning as designed. Which safety lesson best applies?
options: Failure to verify equipment setup/function can create hazards even without intrinsic device malfunction
True device malfunction is the only meaningful equipment risk
Inspired-O2 monitoring is unnecessary after checkout
A successful previous case proves the workstation remains safe
questions.explanation: Most equipment mishaps come from failure to check or unfamiliarity.

questions.stem: A clinician unfamiliar with a ventilator cannot promptly locate or adjust a critical setting during deterioration. Which equipment-safety principle is illustrated?
options: User familiarity and competent operation are essential parts of equipment safety
Modern ventilators are safe regardless of user familiarity
Only biomedical personnel need to understand ventilator controls
Equipment checkout eliminates the need to know how controls work
questions.explanation: Equipment-related mishaps come mostly from unfamiliarity and failure to check, not device malfunction.

questions.stem: Vitals are automatically charted every 5 minutes, but the provider has not directly reassessed the patient, airway, or field for 20 minutes. What principle is being missed?
options: Recorded monitor data do not replace active clinical assessment and interpretation
Five-minute charting eliminates the need for visual assessment
Alarm limits can substitute for situational awareness
questions.explanation: Technology is a tool; patient assessment and interpretation remain essential.

questions.stem: An ETT securing device is compressing the patient's lip beneath the drapes. Which routine assessment should detect this before tissue injury develops?
options: A direct patient sweep for pressure on the nose, lips, eyes, and other vulnerable areas
questions.explanation: The patient sweep includes checking lips and nose for pressure.

questions.stem: The eyelids are not fully closed or protected during GA. Which preventable complication is most directly increased?
questions.explanation: Eyes should be taped and protected.

questions.stem: PIP rises, plateau pressure remains stable, wheezing appears, and the capnogram loses its sharp alpha angle with a prolonged sloped expiratory phase. Which pattern is present?
options: Expiratory airflow obstruction such as bronchospasm
questions.explanation: A shark-fin with absent alpha angle indicates obstruction.

questions.stem: During a long anesthetic, a skin probe reads 34.0 °C while distal esophageal temperature is 36.0 °C. Which value should guide assessment of core temperature?
options: The distal esophageal value because skin temperature does not reliably represent core temperature
The skin value because it detects hypothermia earlier
Neither unless a pulmonary-artery catheter is present
questions.explanation: Skin temperature does not adequately represent mean body temperature.

questions.stem: An esophageal temperature probe is left high in the esophagus near the airway. Why may it poorly represent core temperature?
options: Proximal placement can be influenced by respiratory gases; distal esophageal placement better reflects central temperature
Proximal placement always reads pulmonary-artery temperature
The probe measures skin temperature when placed proximally
Esophageal temperature is never a core measurement
questions.explanation: Distal esophageal placement is needed for core readings.

questions.stem: Core temperature reaches 34 °C during a prolonged operation. Which pair of consequences should be anticipated?
options: Impaired coagulation and prolonged drug effects
Accelerated drug metabolism and reduced bleeding
Improved wound defense and reduced shivering
questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs coagulation and drug metabolism.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 27 mmHg and simultaneous PaCO2 is 31 mmHg with a normal waveform and high minute ventilation. Which interpretation best fits?
options: Marked increase in alveolar dead space
questions.explanation: Low ETCO2 and PaCO2 together indicate hyperventilation.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 45 mmHg and simultaneous PaCO2 is 50 mmHg. How should the arterial-to-end-tidal gradient be interpreted in an otherwise uncomplicated anesthetic?
options: A 5-mmHg gradient is within the expected range
A 5-mmHg gradient proves major dead space
ETCO2 should normally exceed PaCO2 by 5 mmHg
questions.explanation: A 5 mmHg gradient is typical.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 25 mmHg while simultaneous PaCO2 is 50 mmHg despite a sustained capnogram. Which mechanism best explains the 25-mmHg gradient?
options: Markedly increased alveolar dead space or V/Q mismatch
questions.explanation: A large gradient suggests dead space or V/Q mismatch.

questions.stem: PIP rises while plateau pressure remains stable and the capnogram develops a sloped expiratory plateau. What should be assessed first?
options: Airway obstruction from bronchospasm, secretions, or ETT kinking
questions.explanation: Sloping plateau and high PIP suggest obstruction.

questions.stem: Immediately after intubation, no sustained exhaled CO2 is detected. SpO2 remains 100% from preoxygenation. What is the safest response?
options: Assume esophageal placement or failed ventilation until rapidly proven otherwise and re-establish effective ventilation
Wait for SpO2 to fall before acting
Treat bronchospasm before checking tube position
questions.explanation: A flat line after intubation suggests esophageal placement.

questions.stem: A bleeding patient has rapid pressure swings between routine 5-minute cuff measurements and requires repeated vasoactive treatment. How should monitoring be escalated?
options: Increase measurement frequency and strongly consider beat-to-beat invasive arterial monitoring
Keep 5-minute intervals because they satisfy the minimum
Lengthen cuff cycles to avoid compression injury
Use pulse oximetry as the primary pressure trend
questions.explanation: Five minutes is the minimum. Unstable patients need more frequent or invasive monitoring.

questions.stem: Because the upper arm is inaccessible, NIBP is measured at the forearm. How should the result be interpreted?
options: Forearm values may differ systematically from upper-arm measurements and can overestimate BP, so site/cuff limitations should be considered
Forearm BP is always lower than brachial BP
Forearm and upper-arm values are interchangeable regardless of cuff size
Forearm pressure cannot be measured oscillometrically
questions.explanation: Forearm measurements can overestimate BP.

questions.stem: PIP, exhaled tidal volume, and ETCO2 all fall abruptly, followed by decreasing SpO2. Which problem should be checked immediately?
options: A breathing-circuit disconnection or major leak
questions.explanation: Falling PIP and ETCO2 suggest disconnection or leak.

questions.stem: PIP rises abruptly as a lightly anesthetized patient coughs and moves against controlled ventilation; plateau pressure normalizes when coughing stops. Which explanation best fits?
questions.explanation: Coughing or bucking raises PIP.

questions.stem: After sudden unilateral loss of breath sounds, PIP and plateau pressure rise and a pneumothorax is diagnosed. What happens to respiratory-system compliance?
options: It decreases, requiring greater pressure for a given volume
questions.explanation: Pneumothorax decreases compliance.

questions.stem: Pulmonary edema develops and both PIP and plateau pressure rise for the same delivered tidal volume. Which mechanical change is expected?
options: Isolated airway resistance with unchanged compliance
questions.explanation: Pulmonary edema reduces compliance.

questions.stem: In severe emphysema, less elastic recoil allows a given volume at relatively low distending pressure. Which mechanical property is increased?
questions.explanation: Emphysema increases compliance.

questions.stem: After head repositioning, expiratory flow falls and PIP rises while plateau remains stable. Which ventilator display is particularly useful for visualizing the change in airway resistance?
questions.explanation: Flow–volume loops reflect resistance.

questions.stem: After pneumoperitoneum, more pressure is required to deliver the same tidal volume. Which ventilator display most directly demonstrates the change in compliance?
questions.explanation: P–V loops show compliance changes.

questions.stem: ETCO2 rises despite increased minute ventilation, followed by tachycardia and increasing core temperature. Which diagnosis is most concerning?
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 and temperature suggest MH; temperature is a late sign.

questions.stem: While the provider is looking away from the monitor, the pulse-oximeter tone progressively decreases in pitch. What useful information does this convey?
options: A falling oxygen saturation can be recognized acoustically before the numeric display is viewed
questions.explanation: Variable pitch enables early recognition of oxygenation changes.

questions.stem: A high-risk vascular patient is monitored with only one ECG lead throughout the case. What is the major limitation?
options: Ischemic changes outside the territory represented by that lead may be missed
A single lead cannot detect any arrhythmia
ASA standards prohibit displaying a single lead
questions.explanation: Multiple leads improve ischemia detection.

questions.stem: During MAC, ETCO2 abruptly becomes zero with no waveform, but the awake patient continues talking and breathing comfortably. Which cause is most likely?
questions.explanation: A breathing patient with no waveform suggests sampling issues.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 60 mmHg with a normal waveform, slow respiratory rate, and low minute ventilation. Which mechanism best explains the hypercapnia?
questions.explanation: Normal waveform with high ETCO2 and low MV suggests hypoventilation.

questions.stem: ETCO2 remains 60 mmHg despite substantially increased minute ventilation; tachycardia and rising temperature develop. Which mechanism should move higher on the differential?
questions.explanation: High ETCO2 despite high MV suggests increased CO2 production.

questions.stem: A patient on high FiO2 maintains SpO2 100% despite significant underlying shunt physiology. What limitation does this illustrate?
options: A normal saturation on supplemental oxygen does not establish normal pulmonary gas exchange
Pulse oximetry directly quantifies shunt fraction
High FiO2 makes pulse oximetry invalid
questions.explanation: High FiO2 can maintain SpO2 despite shunt.

questions.stem: ETCO2 is 38 mmHg with a normal waveform and SpO2 is 99% in a stable patient. Which conclusion is appropriately limited to these data?
options: Current monitored ventilation and arterial oxygen saturation appear acceptable, but these values do not exclude every respiratory problem
All aspects of pulmonary function are normal
Dead space and shunt are definitively absent
The airway position cannot change while these values remain normal
questions.explanation: Normal ETCO2 and waveform suggest adequate ventilation.

questions.stem: SpO2 reads 95%, but the pleth waveform is weak and erratic in a vasoconstricted patient. What is the best response?
options: Improve perfusion/signal quality and assess the patient before relying on the displayed saturation
Increase FiO2 solely because of the displayed value
Ignore the signal because the number is above 90%
questions.explanation: Interpret SpO2 with signal quality and perfusion.

questions.stem: A NIBP cuff is placed over an upper-arm PICC and repeatedly cycles. Which avoidable problem can result?
options: Compression may obstruct or damage the catheter and interrupt infusion
SpO2 on that arm becomes falsely high
questions.explanation: Avoid cuff placement over PICC lines.

questions.stem: Radial arterial cannulation is considered in a limb with severe peripheral vascular disease and poor distal perfusion. What is the principal concern?
options: Further compromising an already limited arterial supply and increasing ischemic risk
Peripheral vascular disease improves collateral circulation
Stiff vessels guarantee more accurate pressure measurement
There is no additional risk if the catheter is small
questions.explanation: Compromised collateral supply is a contraindication.

questions.stem: The capnogram becomes flat and ETCO2 reads zero at the same moment the patient becomes pulseless. Which physiologic explanation is most likely?
options: Loss of pulmonary blood flow from cardiac arrest
Sampling-line occlusion as the primary explanation
questions.explanation: Pulseless with flat ETCO2 indicates cardiac arrest.

questions.stem: During CPR, ETCO2 abruptly increases from 10 to 35 mmHg without a ventilation change and a pulse becomes detectable. What does the change suggest?
options: Return of spontaneous circulation with increased pulmonary perfusion
questions.explanation: A sudden rise in ETCO2 during CPR suggests improved perfusion or ROSC.

questions.stem: A nasopharyngeal temperature probe is appropriately positioned during GA. How should this site be classified?
options: A site usable only during cardiopulmonary bypass
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is listed among core temperature sites.

questions.stem: Immediately after prone positioning, PIP rises abruptly while plateau pressure remains near baseline. What should be checked first?
options: ETT/circuit kinking, migration, secretions, or other causes of increased airway resistance
Increase FiO2 without assessing the airway
Increase anesthetic depth as the only intervention
questions.explanation: Position changes can dislodge or kink the ETT.

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient with an LMA has ETCO2 55 mmHg, respiratory rate 6/min, and adequate SpO2 on supplemental oxygen. Which response best addresses the primary problem?
options: Support ventilation and correct excessive anesthetic/opioid depression as appropriate
Treat the normal SpO2 as evidence that no intervention is needed
Remove capnography because an LMA is present
questions.explanation: Hypoventilation with an LMA may need assisted ventilation.

questions.stem: After intubation, three sustained exhaled CO2 waveforms are present. What does this finding establish, and what does it not establish?
options: It strongly supports tracheal ventilation but does not confirm optimal ETT depth
It confirms both tracheal placement and ideal depth
questions.explanation: Three stable waveforms support tracheal placement, not depth.

questions.stem: Several alarms activate simultaneously after an abrupt patient change. Which initial strategy is safest?
options: Assess the patient first while rapidly determining whether the alarms share a common oxygenation, ventilation, circulatory, or equipment cause
Silence all alarms before looking at the patient
Address only the first alarm chronologically
questions.explanation: Every alarm must be evaluated, starting with the patient.

questions.stem: Immediately after aortic unclamping, ETCO2 transiently rises despite unchanged ventilation. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Washout of accumulated CO2 from reperfused tissues
questions.explanation: Aortic unclamping transiently raises ETCO2.

questions.stem: Before induction, the Yankauer is present but suction has not been connected or tested. Which preparation failure is most important?
options: Functional suction was not verified before anesthetic induction
The pulse oximeter was not calibrated
questions.explanation: Suction is the "S" in MS MAID.

questions.stem: Before induction, standard intubation equipment is present but no supraglottic rescue airway is immediately available. Which preparation domain is incomplete?
questions.explanation: Airway items include an LMA and other adjuncts.

questions.stem: Before induction of a hemodynamically fragile patient, routine induction drugs are prepared but no rescue vasopressor is immediately available. Which setup domain is incomplete?
questions.explanation: Drugs include emergency medications.

questions.stem: Major blood loss is expected, but no rapid infusion or fluid-warming capability has been prepared. Which setup domain is incomplete?
questions.explanation: IV setup includes warmers and rapid infusers.

questions.stem: A long case with expected temperature change begins without a temperature probe or warming plan. Which preparation domain was inadequately addressed?
questions.explanation: Monitors include temperature when indicated.

questions.stem: A full backup oxygen cylinder is confirmed before the anesthetic. Which workstation-safety function does this provide?
options: An alternate oxygen source if the primary supply fails
questions.explanation: Machine includes the backup O2 cylinder.

questions.stem: During CO2 insufflation, ETCO2 suddenly falls, severe hypotension develops, and a mill-wheel murmur is heard. Which diagnosis best unifies the findings?
questions.explanation: A sudden ETCO2 fall with hypotension and a characteristic murmur during insufflation points to gas embolism.

questions.stem: The arterial line shows a sharp systolic peak of 168 mmHg while NIBP is 138/74; both methods report MAP near 94 mmHg and the invasive system appears underdamped. Which pressure should be weighted most while the system is corrected?
options: MAP, because it is generally less distorted by damping than systolic pressure
The invasive systolic value because invasive measurements are always superior
The NIBP systolic value because cuffs cannot be affected by technical error
questions.explanation: Underdamping inflates SBP, but MAP stays close to true; use MAP while you fix the system.

questions.stem: A curare cleft appears, quantitative TOF is 4/4 with ratio 0.5, and surgery still requires immobility for another 30 minutes. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Titrate additional neuromuscular blocker to surgical need and continue quantitative monitoring
Use extreme volatile depth instead of neuromuscular blockade
Ignore the spontaneous effort because ETCO2 is normal
questions.explanation: Returning effort with inadequate block for surgery calls for a titrated NMB redose guided by monitoring.

questions.stem: During checkout, the oxygen analyzer reads 100% while exposed to room air. What should occur before clinical use?
options: Recalibrate/verify the analyzer and replace the sensor if it cannot correctly read room air
Accept the value as normal for a galvanic cell
Proceed if the pipeline pressure is normal
questions.explanation: Room air should read 21%; a 100% reading means miscalibration.

questions.stem: During rapid rewarming after bypass, bladder temperature is 36.9 °C and rectal temperature is 35.6 °C. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: Rectal temperature can lag during rapid thermal change, so the higher central-site trend may better reflect current rewarming
Rectal temperature is always the instantaneous gold standard
Both values should be averaged equally
The discrepancy proves both probes are malfunctioning
questions.explanation: Rectal temperature lags during active rewarming.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, supplemental oxygen raises SpO2 from 94% to 99%, but ETCO2 remains 52 mmHg and respiratory rate is 7/min. Which problem persists?
options: Alveolar hypoventilation despite improved oxygen saturation
The patient now has increased dead space solely because oxygen was administered
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen corrects SpO2 but not CO2 retention.
